# Reading Journal: Student Guidelines

Grade band: 6 to 8. Voice: direct, short sentences, second person.

This is the student-facing guidelines text. Place it on the module's first page or pin it as a Canvas page. The builder fills the few bracketed course-specific fields.

---

## What the Reading Journal is

Your Reading Journal is one Word document that you keep for the whole module. It is your organizer. Your vocabulary, your reading notes and answers, your notes on how the author writes, and your growing project idea all live in this one file. You build it a little every week.

You do not turn it in every week. Your teacher looks at it closely twice: once around the middle of the module and once at the end. That review is called the Reading Journal Check.

## How to make your copy

1. Open the Reading Journal document for this module from the assignment in Canvas. Word will open your own copy in your school M365 account. 2. If your teacher did not hand you a copy through Canvas, open Word from office.com using your school account (not a personal account), open the module's Reading Journal template, and use File > Save As to make your own copy. 3. Name your file like this: LastName_[COURSECODE]_ReadingJournal_[MODULESHORTNAME]. Example: Garcia_GT_ReadingJournal_Module1.

## Where to save it

Save it in your OneDrive course folder so it is easy to find all module long:

Optima > ELA > [Course_Semester]

Keep the journal in the same folder as your Quick Writes. Do not save it to your desktop or a personal account, and do not start a new copy each week. One document, all module.

## How to add to it each week

  • When a lesson says "Add this to the Week ___ section of your Reading Journal," open your journal and go to that week's block in Section 3.
  • Type your answers under the prompts. Do not erase the prompts; answer beneath them.
  • Add the week's vocabulary to the Section 2 table.
  • Add one new dated line to your Section 1 answer to the Module Question.
  • Drop any craft or character notes into Section 4, and add to your project claim in Section 5 when a Quick Write points you there.
  • OneDrive saves your work automatically and keeps a version history, so you will not lose it.

## What the Reading Journal Check looks at

When your teacher reviews your journal, they read three sections:

  • Section 2 (Word Study): Did you add the words, with meanings in your own words and the lines they came from?
  • Section 3 (Weekly Reading Notes and Responses): Did you answer each week's prompts in full sentences, using details from the reading?
  • Section 5 (Toward the Project): Is your claim taking shape, with evidence attached?

You are graded on completeness and honest effort, not on having a perfect answer. The point is steady building. If a week is thin, the check is your signal to catch it up before the project.

Quick reminder: one document, kept in your OneDrive course folder, added to every week. That is the whole habit.

RESEARCH AND JSTOR ACCESS
Finding real sources, and knowing they are real
JStor is a large library of articles that scholars have checked before publishing. This page shows you how to get in. Keep it bookmarked; you will come back to it whenever a lesson asks you to find a source.
🔑 HOW TO LOG IN (OPTIMA SHARED ACCESS)

Go to www.jstor.org and sign in with the Optima account below. This account is for Optima students' coursework only. Please do not share it with anyone outside the school.

Username: optimaonline
Password: wisdom359

There is no separate "off campus" step. This is the same login whether you are at home or anywhere else, because Optima is an online school.

📚 TWO PLACES, ONE LIBRARY
STEP 1 · JSTOR DAILY
daily.jstor.org. No login needed. Short, readable articles written for anyone, and every one links to the real research behind it.
STEP 2 · JSTOR
jstor.org, signed in with the login above. This is the full library: the scholarly article itself, and thousands more like it.
🔍 SEARCH WELL
Use two or three key words, not a full question. "Klondike sled dogs" finds more than "how did dogs help people during the gold rush."
Read the short summary at the top of an article (the abstract) before opening the whole thing. It tells you fast whether the source fits.
⚠️ WORTH KNOWING · AI AND SOURCES
An AI tool can help you turn a question into search words. It cannot tell you what articles actually exist, and it sometimes invents titles and authors that sound real but are not. Only ever use a source you found and opened on JStor yourself.

# The Outsiders: Reading Journal / Module Organizer (M365 Word doc spec)

Module 4 instance, built from the course-shared TEMPLATE. This is the exact spec for the Word document each student copies at the start of Module 4 and keeps in the OneDrive course folder. Hand it out through the Canvas + OneDrive LTI assignment so each student gets their own copy. The five fixed sections match every module of the course.

Hard rules. No em dashes in student-facing text. Name craft terms plainly. Dates carry A.D. or B.C. where relevant.

\---

\\\\\\\\\\\\\\NOTICE:\\\\\\\\\\\\\\ Students must obtain lawful access to the assigned literary work separately. Optima course materials are original instructional materials designed to support analysis, discussion, and assessment of the work. Copyrighted text, images, audio, or other protected materials are not reproduced here except where expressly licensed, in the public domain, or used as a limited fair-use excerpt for instructional analysis.

\---

## Document setup and layout

  • File type: Microsoft Word (.docx), from the student's school M365 account.
  • File name: LastName\\\\\\\_OS\\\\\\\_ReadingJournal\\\\\\\_Module4 (example: Garcia\\\\\\\_OS\\\\\\\_ReadingJournal\\\\\\\_Module4).
  • Save location: Optima > ELA > \\\\\\\[Course\\\\\\\_Semester] in OneDrive.
  • Font: Calibri 11 or Times New Roman 12.
  • Headings: Word Heading 1 for each Section; Heading 2 for each week block in Section 3.
  • Page numbers: bottom of the page.
  • Tables: real Word tables for Section 2 and the Section 3 blocks.

M365 Skill You're Practicing: Applying Heading Styles and Inserting a Table (Word).

\---

## COVER (first page)

  • Course: 7th Grade English Language Arts
  • Module: Module 4, The Outsiders (S. E. Hinton, 1967)
  • Student name: \[student types]
  • Module Question / Theme: What divides the greasers and the Socs, and what does the novel say stays the same on both sides?

Center the block; course name largest; module question in italics beneath.

\\\\\\\\\\\\\\NOTICE:\\\\\\\\\\\\\\ Students must obtain lawful access to the assigned literary work separately. Optima course materials are original instructional materials designed to support analysis, discussion, and assessment of the work. Copyrighted text, images, audio, or other protected materials are not reproduced here except where expressly licensed, in the public domain, or used as a limited fair-use excerpt for instructional analysis.

\---

## SECTION 1: Module Question (your evolving answer)

Heading 1: Section 1, Module Question

The big question for this module is below. You will answer it many times. Do not erase old answers. Add a new dated line each week so you can watch your thinking change.

Module Question: What divides the greasers and the Socs, and what does the novel say stays the same on both sides?

  • Week 1 answer (date): \_\_\_\_\_\_\_
  • Week 2 answer (date): \_\_\_\_\_\_\_
  • Week 3 answer (date): \_\_\_\_\_\_\_
  • Week 4 answer (date): \_\_\_\_\_\_\_
  • Week 5 answer (date): \_\_\_\_\_\_\_
  • Week 6 answer (date): \_\_\_\_\_\_\_
  • Final answer before the project (date): \_\_\_\_\_\_\_

\---

## SECTION 2: Word Study

Heading 1: Section 2, Word Study

Each week you study a small set of words from the reading. Add every word to the table below. Write what it means in your own words, and copy the exact line from your copy of the book where you met it (write the chapter number too).

Insert one Word table with these exact headers, pre-loaded with a divider row per week and empty rows for each word:

|Word|What it means (in your own words)|The line it came from (with chapter)| |-|-|-|

Pre-load these week labels and words (meanings are starter glosses; students rewrite in their own words):

  • Week 1, Ch. 1-2: menacing, stylized, rivalry, incredulous, rueful
  • Week 2, Ch. 3-4: premonition, recklessly, sophisticated, defiant, conviction
  • Week 3, Ch. 5-6: reluctant, gallant, sullen, unfathomable, roguishly
  • Week 4, Ch. 7-8: doggedly, fiercely, grim, remorseful, wistful
  • Week 5, Ch. 9-10: imploringly, falter, resigned, hysterics, vaguely
  • Week 6, Ch. 11-12: aloof, profound, contented, wisely, empathy

\---

## SECTION 3: Weekly Reading Notes and Responses

Heading 1: Section 3, Weekly Reading Notes and Responses

This is the heart of your journal. There is one block per week. When a lesson says "Add this to the Week \\\\\\\_\\\\\\\_\\\\\\\_ section of your Reading Journal," this is where it goes. Each week block has two parts: the reading-response prompts (answer these in full sentences) and a space for your own notes.

Create one Heading 2 block per week, exactly as below.

### Heading 2: Week 1, Ch. 1-2

Reading-response prompts (answer in full sentences):

1. In your own words, describe the difference between the greasers and the Socs as Ponyboy explains it in Chapter 1. What does each group have, and what does each group lack? 2. Ponyboy narrates the story from inside his own group. Give one example from Chapters 1 or 2 where you can tell he is presenting his side sympathetically. What clue in his word choice shows this? 3. The gang treats Ponyboy and Soda differently from the way their school or the Socs treat them. What does the novel seem to be saying about where a person finds belonging?

My reading notes (characters, surprising lines, questions): \_\_\_\_\_\_\_

### Heading 2: Week 2, Ch. 3-4

Reading-response prompts (answer in full sentences):

1. Describe the events that force Johnny and Ponyboy to run. Stick to what happens in the novel without quoting it directly. Why does Johnny make the choice he makes? 2. In your own words, explain why the greasers are loyal to each other even when it puts them in danger. Use one specific moment from Chapters 3 or 4 as your example. 3. Was what Johnny did self-defense, or something else? State your position in a sentence, then give one reason from the story that supports it.

My reading notes: \_\_\_\_\_\_\_

### Heading 2: Week 3, Ch. 5-6

Reading-response prompts (answer in full sentences):

📖 THIS WEEK’S WORDS
heater (slang: a firearm or weapon): a gun, especially in street or gang contexts. Example: The officer reached for his gear before stepping outside.
roughneck (a tough, working-class person known for physical toughness): someone without much polish who does hard, manual work. Example: The recruiter wanted roughnecks who could handle the difficult conditions of the work site.
gallant (brave, polite, and honorable, especially toward others): showing courage or noble behavior. Example: The firefighter made a gallant effort to save the dog from the burning building.
savvy (having practical understanding or good judgment): being smart about how things work in the real world. Example: She was savvy enough to know when an argument was no longer worth having.
incredulous (not willing or able to believe something; showing strong disbelief): Example: He stared at the scoreboard with an incredulous expression, unable to accept that his team had lost.
🌱 WORD ROOTS
savvy comes from the Latin verb sapere, meaning “to know” or “to taste.” Savvy kept that old sense of really knowing how something works.
incredulous breaks into two Latin pieces: the prefix in-, meaning “not,” and cred, from credere, meaning “to believe.” Put together, the word literally means “not believing,” which fits someone who cannot accept what they are seeing.
🔍 BEFORE YOU’RE TOLD: CONTEXT CLUES
Before you look at the meaning above, what in the surrounding words hints at what roughneck means? Check the words around it in the example sentence before you check the definition.

Your rewrite: “She was wise enough to recognize the moment when continuing to argue would accomplish nothing.”
3
Write one final sentence of your own using any one of the five words in a way that connects to the theme of two groups divided by background or experience.

🔮 WHAT YOU ARE DOING
In VR Activity 1 you built a scene showing two divided worlds from a distance. This second activity goes deeper: you will set up a single shared setting and then step into it from two different perspectives, using annotations and symbolic objects to show how the same space can look and feel completely different depending on who is standing in it. This feeds your Module 4 project. Save your work.
📋 WHAT YOU WILL NEED

Set up one shared setting in the middle of your virtual space. This represents neutral ground: a street corner, a park, a doorway, or any space two different kinds of people might both pass through. Use available objects to mark it clearly as a shared, central location.
2
Place three symbolic objects in the central space. Choose objects that could mean something different depending on who is looking. For example: a streetlight, a fence post, a crumpled newspaper. 📖 THIS WEEK'S WORDS
Five words appear in Chapters 3 and 4 of The Outsiders. Study each word, its meaning, and where it comes up in those chapters.
1. rebellious (adjective)
Refusing to follow rules or accept authority; resisting control.
Chapter 3. The tension between the greasers and the Socs reflects a rebellious streak that runs through the whole group's way of life.
2. gallant (adjective)
Brave and noble in a way that shows concern for others; courageous.
Chapter 3. The word surfaces when characters reflect on what it means to act with courage under pressure, on what real bravery looks like.
3. imploringly (adverb)
In a way that begs or pleads urgently; asking with desperation.
Chapter 4. The adverb appears at a moment of crisis when a character turns to another for help, unable to hide how desperate the situation has become.
4. premonition (noun)
A feeling that something, often something bad, is about to happen.
Chapter 3. The feeling of unease building through Chapter 3 gives Ponyboy what might be called a premonition, a quiet sense that things are about to go wrong.
5. self-preservation (noun)
The instinct to protect oneself from harm or death.
Chapter 4. After the crisis at the end of Chapter 4, the choices the characters make are driven partly by self-preservation, the need to stay safe at any cost.
🌱 WORD ROOTS
rebellious comes from the Latin re- (“again”) plus bellum (“war”). To rebel originally meant to go to war again, to rise up a second time against someone in charge, which is close to the modern sense of refusing to follow rules.

imploringly comes from Latin im- (a form of “in”) plus plorare, meaning “to cry out or weep.” Someone acting imploringly is, by the word’s roots, calling out with something close to tears.

premonition comes from Latin prae- (“before”) plus monere (“to warn”). A premonition is a warning that arrives before the thing it warns about.
🔍 BEFORE YOU'RE TOLD: CONTEXT CLUES
Before you look at the meaning above, what in the surrounding words hints at what self-preservation means? Look at how the phrase is used in the sentence before you check the definition.

🔒 COPYRIGHT NOTICE
Students must obtain lawful access to the assigned literary work separately. Optima course materials are original instructional materials designed to support analysis, discussion, and assessment of the work. Copyrighted text, images, audio, or other protected materials are not reproduced here except where expressly licensed, in the public domain, or used as a limited fair-use excerpt for instructional analysis.
🎯 THE IDEA

Every character in The Outsiders faces moments where they have to choose. Some choices are fast and desperate. Others build slowly over several chapters. In both cases, the choice is a window: it shows you something about who the character is and what they value.

This week you will write one analytical claim about a character's choice from Chapters 3 or 4. A claim is not a summary. It is a position that someone could argue against, backed by at least one specific detail.

📝 STUDENT DIRECTIONS
1
Choose one character from Chapters 3 or 4 and one specific choice that character makes. You can use a choice from Chapter 3, the crisis decision in Chapter 4, or the choice to run and seek help at the end of Chapter 4. The choice is yours.
2

Write a claim: one sentence that says what that choice reveals about the character. Your claim should be specific enough that someone could disagree with it. Do not write a summary of what happened. Write what you think it means.

Here is the difference:

Summary: “In Chapter 4, Johnny and Ponyboy face a serious situation and have to make a quick decision.”

Claim: “Johnny's decision in Chapter 4 shows that his loyalty to Ponyboy outweighs any concern for his own safety or future.”

(The claim takes a position. The summary just describes.)

3
Write 150–200 words that develop your claim. Include: what the character chose, one specific detail from the chapter that supports your reading (describe it in your own words), and one sentence that explains what this choice says about the character's values. Do not copy sentences from the novel.
4

These five words appear in Chapters 5–6. Each definition below is in Optima’s own words. Find where the word appears in your copy of the novel; do not copy the surrounding text.

elude (to escape from or avoid someone or something by being quick or clever).
sullen (gloomily silent and withdrawn, refusing to speak or cooperate).

contemptuously comes from Latin com- (an intensifying prefix) plus temnere (“to scorn or despise”). Someone acting contemptuously is, at the word’s root, showing full scorn for someone else.

📖 THIS WEEK'S WORDS (look them up as you encounter them in your reading)
sullenly (in a resentful, sulky, silent way): used to describe a mood that is unhappy but held inward rather than expressed openly.
bewildering (confusing in a way that is hard to sort out): when something happens too fast or strangely for you to make sense of it.
defiance (open refusal to obey or accept authority): a deliberate act of standing against someone who has power over you.
incredulous (unwilling or unable to believe something): a reaction of disbelief, usually because something seems too surprising to be true.
gallant (brave and honorable, especially in the face of difficulty): showing courage and dignity; often used to describe a way of carrying oneself under pressure.
🌱 WORD ROOTS
sullenly comes from Latin solus, meaning “alone.” The word first described a person keeping to themselves, and that sense of pulling away is still part of what sullenly describes today.
defiance comes from Latin dis- (“apart, away”) plus fidere (“to trust”). Defiance, at its root, means breaking away from trust or loyalty, refusing to go along with someone in charge.
incredulous breaks into Latin in- (“not”) plus cred, from credere (“to believe”). It literally means “not believing.”

Your rewrite: He sat in silence, his face dark, refusing to talk to anyone.
3
Write one new sentence of your own using any one of the five words correctly.

📖 READING ASSIGNMENT
Read Chapters 9-10 in your copy of The Outsiders.

ⓘ REQUIRED NOTICE
Students must obtain lawful access to the assigned literary work separately. Optima course materials are original instructional materials designed to support analysis, discussion, and assessment of the work. Copyrighted text, images, audio, or other protected materials are not reproduced here except where expressly licensed, in the public domain, or used as a limited fair-use excerpt for instructional analysis.
📖 READ & NOTICE · FIVE WORDS FROM CHAPTERS 9-10

These five words come up in the kinds of intense, emotionally charged situations that mark chapters like these. Add all five to your Reading Journal before you begin the steps below.

valor
Meaning: Courage in the face of danger: the willingness to act even when you are afraid.
A word that fits events like those in Chapters 9-10, where characters are tested under pressure and must decide how to respond.
contempt
Meaning: A feeling that someone or something is beneath you; a kind of scornful disgust toward a person or idea.
A word that fits events like those in Chapters 9-10, where rivalry and group loyalty push characters toward dismissing each other entirely.
resigned
Meaning: Accepting something difficult or painful without fighting it; giving in to what cannot be changed.
A word that fits events like those in Chapters 9-10, where characters face losses they cannot undo and must find a way to carry on.
realization
Meaning: The moment when something important becomes completely clear to you; the act of understanding something for the first time.
A word that fits events like those in Chapters 9-10, where a character might suddenly grasp the full weight of what has happened.
hysterical
Meaning: In a state of extreme, uncontrolled emotion: laughing or crying or reacting in a way that cannot be held back.
A word that fits events like those in Chapters 9-10, where shock and grief can push someone past the point of staying composed.
🌱 WORD ROOTS
valor comes from the Latin verb valere, meaning “to be strong” or “to be worth.” Valor is a strength of character, the kind that lets someone act even when scared.

resigned comes from Latin re- (“back”) plus signare (“to seal or mark”). To resign originally meant to unseal or cancel something formally; being resigned to a hard situation means you have stopped fighting it and accepted it as final.

hysterical comes from the Greek word hystera, meaning “womb.” Ancient doctors wrongly believed uncontrollable emotion came from the womb, which is where this now-outdated idea behind the word’s origin comes from.
🔍 BEFORE YOU'RE TOLD: CONTEXT CLUES
Before you look at the meaning above, what in the sentence hints at what contempt means? Notice how it is connected to rivalry and group loyalty before you check the definition.
📋 ASSIGNMENT OVERVIEW
You will record this week's five vocabulary words in your Reading Journal and then practice them in your own writing. The goal is to use each word accurately enough that it shows you understand it, not just that you can copy a definition.
🎯 FOCUS QUESTION
How precisely can you use a word when the context is yours to invent?
📝 STUDENT DIRECTIONS
1
Add all five words and their meanings to the Word Study section of your Reading Journal. Write the word and the meaning in your own words.
2
Pick three of the five words. For each one, write one original sentence using the word correctly in a context that is not from the novel. Your sentence should show the meaning through context, not just repeat the definition.
MODEL SENTENCE
"She felt a deep realization that her plan had never been as solid as she believed."
Notice: the model does not quote the novel. It invents a situation that shows what the word means.
3
Write a short paragraph of 3-5 sentences describing a moment of courage or change. Choose any topic you like: it does not have to connect to the novel. Use at least two of the five words naturally within your paragraph.
✅ SUCCESS CRITERIA

☐

Week 6
Word Study: Words from the Final Chapters
Assignment · 10 pts · about 18 minutes
📖 THIS WEEK'S WORDS (own-words definitions; locate each word in Chapters 11–12 of your copy)
bewildered (completely confused and unable to understand what is happening)
resigned (accepting something difficult or unwanted without fighting it)
contemptuously (in a way that shows you think someone or something is worthless or beneath you)
imploring (begging with great urgency and emotion)
sullenly (in a moody, silent, bad-tempered way)
Locate each word in your copy of Chapters 11 and 12. Record the page number in your Reading Journal alongside the word.
🌱 WORD ROOTS
resigned comes from Latin re- (“back”) plus signare (“to seal or mark”). To resign originally meant to unseal or cancel something formally; being resigned to something hard means accepting it as final.
contemptuously comes from Latin com- (an intensifying prefix) plus temnere (“to scorn or despise”). At its root, acting contemptuously means showing full scorn for someone.
imploring comes from Latin im- (a form of “in”) plus plorare (“to cry out or weep”). Imploring someone means calling out to them with something close to tears.
🔍 BEFORE YOU'RE TOLD: CONTEXT CLUES
Before you look at the meaning above, what in the surrounding sentence hints at what bewildered means? Think about what is happening around a character before you check the definition.
📝 STUDENT DIRECTIONS
1
Add all five words, their own-words meanings, and the page number where you found each one to the Word Study section of your Reading Journal.
2

🔮 WHAT YOU ARE DOING
The idea of staying gold runs through the whole novel. In this activity you will build a thematic arrangement in VR using symbolic objects and your own written labels. FINAL PROJECT · PART 2 OF 2
The Outsiders: Your Creative Piece and VR Scene
Creative piece (your choice) + VR thematic scene + reflection · spread across the project window
🎨 WHAT YOU ARE MAKING
Your essay makes the case for your theme in words. This half of the project lets you show the same idea in a different form. You will create one piece that explores the novel's themes of loyalty, family, or class division, then build a short VR scene that captures something the theme means to you, and write a reflection connecting both.
🖌 PART A: YOUR CREATIVE PIECE (choose one)
Pick whichever format fits what you want to say about the novel's themes:
Option 1: Character Collage (ELA.7.C.5.1)
Build a collage that represents one or more characters from the novel. Use images, colors, symbols, words, or textures that stand for that character's values, loyalties, or place in the greaser-Soc world. Your collage can be made by hand (photographs of a physical piece are fine) or created digitally using any tool you have access to. The collage should be readable: a viewer should be able to look at it and understand something about the character and a theme of the novel.
Option 2: Short Social-Issue Research Piece (ELA.7.C.4.1)
*The Outsiders* was written in 1967 and deals with real social tensions: class, identity, and youth. Research one real social issue the novel touches on (for example, how class or neighborhood shapes the opportunities available to young people, or the role of chosen family in communities where biological family is absent or troubled). Write a short piece (about 200 to 300 words) that explains what you found and connects it to a theme in the novel. Use at least two reliable sources, and cite each one. Write in your own words.
Both options are equal in difficulty and graded on the same rubric. Choose the one that fits what you want to express.
🔮 PART B: YOUR VR THEMATIC SCENE
You have already built VR scenes in this module that explored the novel's world through its themes. Now use your VR headset to build one final thematic scene that shows what a theme from *The Outsiders* means to you. This is not a recreation of the novel's events or characters. It is your own conceptual space built around an idea the novel explores.
📝 IN YOUR VR SETTING, DO THIS
1
Put on your VR headset and open the virtual environment. Choose any setting you like that feels right for the theme you want to show.
2
Build a space that represents your theme. You might use objects, shapes, or labels that stand for loyalty, division, family, or what it means to hold on to something good. You are not staging a scene from the book; you are building something that expresses the theme's meaning to you.
3
Add two labels or sticky notes in the virtual environment. One names the theme your scene represents. The other explains one specific choice you made and why it fits the theme.
4
Record a short video or take a screenshot inside VR that captures your scene and the labels. If VR is not available to you, write a short paragraph (about 100 words) describing the scene you would build and why.
5
Add a spoken explanation, 30 to 60 seconds long: narrate what your scene shows, in order, and name the one key point it makes about the theme you chose. Record this narration as part of your video, or as a short stand-alone audio or video clip if you captured a screenshot or wrote a description instead. This spoken part is required and graded for everyone; it does not trade off against a silent screenshot.
📝 PART C: YOUR REFLECTION (200 to 250 words)
Write a reflection of 200 to 250 words in Word. Answer these questions: What theme did you choose, and what did you learn about it by making your creative piece and VR scene? How did working with the theme in a different form change or deepen how you think about it? What do you still find hard or uncertain about this theme in the novel?

☐

FINAL PROJECT · PART 1 OF 2
The Outsiders: Your Literary-Analysis Essay
Literary-analysis essay · about 500 to 700 words · about 70 minutes of writing time, spread out · built from Quick Writes 3 to 6
📖 WHAT YOU ARE WRITING ABOUT
S. E. Hinton builds her novel around a world divided by class, neighborhood, and appearance. But underneath that division, the novel keeps showing something that persists on both sides: loyalty to people you care about, the pull of family (chosen or given), and the desire to hold on to something good before it slips away. You have been building your analysis through Quick Writes 3, 4, 5, and 6. Now you pull that work into one clear literary-analysis essay.
🎯 FOCUS QUESTION
What does *The Outsiders* say about loyalty, family, or what it means to stay gold, and how does Hinton build that idea across the novel?
📋 ASSIGNMENT OVERVIEW
Write a literary-analysis essay that answers the focus question. Choose one theme (loyalty, family, or staying gold) and make a claim about what the novel says about it. Support your claim with evidence from your own copy of the book, explain how each piece of evidence proves your point, and close with a conclusion. Build it from your Quick Write 3 to 6 work in Section 5 of your Reading Journal. This is one half of your project; the creative and VR half is a separate assignment.
📝 STUDENT DIRECTIONS
1
Choose your theme and write your thesis. Pick one theme to analyze: loyalty, family, or staying gold. Write one clear sentence that states what *The Outsiders* says about that theme. This is your thesis. Put it at the end of a short opening paragraph that sets up the question.
2
Give your evidence and explain it. Use two or three specific events, details, or brief references from your own copy of the book that support your thesis. Cite each one in MLA format: Hinton’s last name plus the chapter, for example (Hinton, Ch. 8). If you already name Hinton in your sentence, just give the chapter. After each one, write a sentence or two that shows how it proves your point. Do not just name the event; explain what it means for your claim. Pull these from Section 5 of your Reading Journal.
3
Write a conclusion. End with two or three sentences that restate your thesis in fresh words and say what Hinton seems to want readers to understand about the theme you chose.
4
Add your Works Cited entry. At the end of your document, add one entry for the novel: Hinton, S. E. The Outsiders. 1967.
5
Be honest about your reasoning. If a detail only partly fits your claim, say so. If the novel seems to say two things at once about your theme, acknowledge that. Naming where your evidence is strong and where it is less certain makes your essay stronger, not weaker.

assignments.html:
# A Midsummer Night's Dream: Reading Journal / Module Organizer (M365 Word doc spec)

Module 4B instance, built from the course-shared TEMPLATE. This is the exact spec for the Word document each student copies at the start of Module 4B and keeps in the OneDrive course folder. Hand it out through the Canvas + OneDrive LTI assignment so each student gets their own copy. The five fixed sections match every module of the course.

Hard rules. No em dashes in student-facing text. Name craft terms plainly. Dates carry A.D. or B.C. where relevant. Cite the play in MLA format: Shakespeare's name plus act.scene (for example, Shakespeare, 1.1), not by page number. If Shakespeare is already named in the sentence, just give the act and scene.

---

## Document setup and layout

  • File type: Microsoft Word (.docx), from the student's school M365 account.
  • File name: LastName_MND_ReadingJournal_Module4B (example: Garcia_MND_ReadingJournal_Module4B).
  • Save location: Optima > ELA > [Course_Semester] in OneDrive.
  • Font: Calibri 11 or Times New Roman 12.
  • Headings: Word Heading 1 for each Section; Heading 2 for each week block in Section 3.
  • Page numbers: bottom of the page.
  • Tables: real Word tables for Section 2 and the Section 3 blocks.

M365 Skill You're Practicing: Applying Heading Styles and Inserting a Table (Word).

---

## COVER (first page)

  • Course: 7th Grade English Language Arts
  • Module: Module 4B, A Midsummer Night's Dream (William Shakespeare, public domain)
  • Student name: [student types]
  • Module Question / Theme: Everyone in this play tells a story about what happened in the wood. Whose account can we trust, and how would we know?

Center the block; course name largest; module question in italics beneath.

---

## SECTION 1: Module Question (your evolving answer)

Heading 1: Section 1, Module Question

The big question for this module is below. You will answer it many times. Do not erase old answers. Add a new dated line each week so you can watch your thinking change.

Module Question: Everyone in this play tells a story about what happened in the wood. Whose account can we trust, and how would we know?

  • Week 1 answer (date): _______
  • Week 2 answer (date): _______
  • Week 3 answer (date): _______
  • Week 4 answer (date): _______
  • Week 5 answer (date): _______
  • Week 6 answer (date): _______
  • Final answer before the project (date): _______

---

## SECTION 2: Word Study

Heading 1: Section 2, Word Study

Each week you study a small set of words from the play. Add every word to the table below. Write what it means in your own words, and copy the exact line where you met it, cited in MLA format: Shakespeare's name plus act.scene (for example, Shakespeare, 1.1).

Insert one Word table with these exact headers, pre-loaded with a divider row per week and empty rows for each word:

|Word|What it means (in your own words)|Where it came from (Shakespeare, act.scene)| |-|-|-|

Pre-load these week labels and words (meanings are starter glosses; students rewrite in their own words; all words are drawn directly from the assigned scenes):

  • Week 1, Act 1 (both scenes): vexation, entreat, beseech, austerity, abjure
  • Week 2, Act 2 (both scenes): forsworn, dissension, changeling, amorous, distemperature
  • Week 3, Act 3 Sc. 1-2: translated, monstrous, amiable, enamour'd, parlous
  • Week 4, Act 4: amazedly, overbear, undistinguishable, solemnity, bethink
  • Week 5, Act 5 Sc. 1 (to the play-within-a-play): compact, frenzy, abridgment, discretion, beguile
  • Week 6, Act 5 Sc. 1 (end) and Epilogue: fordone, hallow'd, reprehend, amends, palpable

---

## SECTION 3: Weekly Reading Notes and Responses

Heading 1: Section 3, Weekly Reading Notes and Responses

This is the heart of your journal. There is one block per week. When a lesson says "Add this to the Week ___ section of your Reading Journal," this is where it goes. Each week block has two parts: the reading-response prompts (answer these in full sentences) and a space for your own notes.

Create one Heading 2 block per week, exactly as below.

### Heading 2: Week 1, Act 1 (both scenes)

Reading-response prompts (answer in full sentences):

1. In Act 1, Scene 1, Egeus tells Theseus a story about how Lysander won Hermia's heart. In your own words, describe how Egeus narrates that courtship. What word choices make his account sound like an accusation rather than a neutral report? 2. Theseus rules that Hermia must obey her father or face death or a life apart from society. What does this ruling suggest about the law in Athens at the start of the play? Cite where Theseus states the ruling, in MLA format (Shakespeare, act.scene). 3. Hermia and Lysander decide to run away together rather than accept Theseus's ruling. In your own words, what does their choice suggest about how they see the difference between the law and what is right?

My reading notes (characters, surprising lines, questions): _______

### Heading 2: Week 2, Act 2 (both scenes)

Reading-response prompts (answer in full sentences):

1. Setting changes people in this play. Once the characters enter the wood, how does the mood of the play shift from the opening scene in Athens? Give one specific detail that shows the change. 2. Titania tells Oberon two stories in Act 2, Scene 1: one about the changeling boy's mother, and one blaming their quarrel for the ruined seasons. In your own words, summarize each story. Do you think either one is meant to be taken as simple fact, or as an argument dressed up as a story? Explain, with a citation. 3. Oberon sets the love-juice plot in motion after Puck brings him the flower. Describe the first mistake that results from it. Whose fault is it, in your view: Puck's, Oberon's, or the situation itself? State your position with a reason.

My reading notes: _______

### Heading 2: Week 3, Act 3 Sc. 1-2

Reading-response prompts (answer in full sentences):

1. This week's lessons cover how the play sounds: verse for the nobles and lovers, and prose for the workmen. Choose one short passage from Act 3 and identify whether it is verse or prose. What does that choice suggest about who is speaking? 2. Bottom is transformed and Titania falls in love with him. In your own words, why is this funny to the audience even though Titania does not know it is strange? What does the scene ask us to notice about how love can misjudge what it sees? 3. Helena describes her childhood friendship with Hermia as "two lovely berries moulded on one stem" (Shakespeare, 3.2). In your own words, what is she using this memory to argue for in the present moment? Is a narrated past a fair kind of evidence to use in an argument? Explain.

My reading notes: _______

### Heading 2: Week 4, Act 4

Reading-response prompts (answer in full sentences):

1. Describe the waking and the undoing in Act 4: how does Oberon set things right, and in what order? Cite one line that shows the moment the enchantments are lifted. 2. Bottom wakes and says, "I have had a most rare vision," then decides he cannot describe it and will have it turned into a ballad instead. In your own words, why might Bottom give up on telling his own story directly? What does that choice suggest about some experiences being hard to put into words? 3. This week you also practiced citing a play in MLA format (Shakespeare's name plus act.scene). Choose one moment from Act 4 and write a full sentence of evidence with a correct citation, followed by one sentence explaining what it shows.

My reading notes: _______

### Heading 2: Week 5, Act 5 Sc. 1 (to the play-within-a-play)

Reading-response prompts (answer in full sentences):

1. Theseus dismisses the lovers' account of the night as the imagining of "the lunatic, the lover, and the poet" (Shakespeare, 5.1). Hippolyta answers that the story "grows to something of great constancy" (Shakespeare, 5.1). In your own words, summarize each position. Whose reasoning do you find more convincing, and why? 2. The mechanicals perform Pyramus and Thisbe for the court. In your own words, describe one specific way their storytelling goes wrong. What does the failure suggest about what a story needs in order to work? 3. This week you also began a counterclaim for your project essay. Write one sentence naming a reason someone might trust a different character's account than the one you plan to argue for, and one sentence explaining why your case still holds.

My reading notes: _______

### Heading 2: Week 6, Act 5 Sc. 1 (end) and Epilogue

Reading-response prompts (answer in full sentences):

1. Puck's epilogue asks the audience to think of the whole play as a dream if it has offended them. In your own words, what does this do to how we should judge everything that came before it, including all the characters' competing stories? 2. This module has compared Puck's epilogue to how Sam McGee's poem opens and closes on the same stanza (Module 2, Week 5). In one or two sentences, explain what a frame does for a story, using either example. 3. Look back across the whole play. Which character's account of the night in the wood do you currently trust the most, and which do you trust the least? Give one reason for each, cited in MLA format (Shakespeare's name plus act.scene).

My reading notes: _______

---

## SECTION 4: Craft, Characters, Theme (running notes)

Heading 1: Section 4, Craft, Characters, Theme

Use this section all module long. When a lesson names a craft move (verse versus prose, allusion, irony) or you notice how a character's story compares to what actually happened, add a short note here with the citation. You will pull from this section when you build your project.

  • Craft moves I noticed: (term, what it was, the citation)
  • Characters and the stories they tell: (character, what they claimed, what the audience actually saw, the citation)
  • Classical allusions I noticed: (the reference, for example Cupid, Diana, or Pyramus and Thisbe, and what it adds to the scene)
  • Theme ideas: (a big idea the play seems to be building about storytelling or belief, and one detail that supports it)

---

## SECTION 5: Toward the Project (your developing claim)

Heading 1: Section 5, Toward the Project

Your module project asks you to make a claim about whose account of the night in the wood deserves belief and back it up with evidence cited from the play. Build that claim here, a little at a time, using your Quick Writes (especially Quick Writes 3, 4, 5, and 6). By the end you should have a claim plus two or three pieces of cited evidence.

  • The project question: By the end of the play, whose account of the night in the wood should we believe, and what does the play suggest about why people tell the stories they tell?
  • My claim (a sentence that answers the question): _______
  • Evidence 1 (a specific moment, cited Shakespeare, act.scene): _______ . Why it supports my claim: _______
  • Works Cited entry (add once, at the end): _Shakespeare, William. A Midsummer Night's Dream._
  • Evidence 2: _______ . Why it supports my claim: _______
  • Evidence 3 (optional): _______ . Why it supports my claim: _______
  • A reason someone might disagree, and my response: _______

---

## Reminder line for the bottom of the document

Keep this document in your OneDrive course folder all module long. Your teacher reviews Sections 2, 3, and 5 at the Reading Journal Check (around Week 3-4 and at the end of the module). You are not turning it in every week; you are building it every week.

📖 THIS WEEK’S WORDS
vexation (a state of being annoyed or troubled): Egeus: “Full of vexation come I, with complaint / Against my child, my daughter Hermia.”
entreat (to ask someone earnestly or respectfully): Hermia: “I do entreat your Grace to pardon me.”
beguil’d (tricked or deceived): Helena: “And therefore is love said to be a child, / Because in choice he is so oft beguil’d.”
extempore (done without preparation, on the spot): Quince: “You may do it extempore, for it is nothing but roaring.”
discretion (careful, sensible judgment about what to say or do): Bottom: “they would have no more discretion but to hang us.”
🌱 WORD ROOTS
vexation comes from the Latin verb vexare, meaning “to shake, jolt, or trouble.” A vexation is something that keeps shaking up your peace of mind.
extempore comes directly from the Latin phrase ex tempore, literally “out of the time.” Something done extempore is done right in the moment, with no time set aside to prepare it.
🔍 BEFORE YOU’RE TOLD: CONTEXT CLUES
Before you look at the meaning above, what in the surrounding words hints at what discretion means? Look at what the craftsmen fear will happen if they frighten the ladies. What quality would have stopped them from making that mistake?

Word Study: Words from Act 2
Assignment · ~18 min · 10 pts
📖 THIS WEEK’S WORDS
changeling (a child secretly exchanged for another, in old folk belief): a human child fairies were said to take, sometimes leaving one of their own in its place. Source line (Puck, Act 2, Scene 1): “She never had so sweet a changeling.”
wanton (reckless or unruly; acting without restraint): behaving without care for consequences or authority. Source line (Oberon, Act 2, Scene 1): “Tarry, rash wanton; am not I thy lord?”
forgeries (false things made to deceive): things falsely shaped or invented to trick someone into believing them. Source line (Titania, Act 2, Scene 1): “These are the forgeries of jealousy.”
distemperature (a disturbance or imbalance, especially in weather or health): a condition thrown out of its normal, healthy balance. Source line (Titania, Act 2, Scene 1): “And thorough this distemperature we see.”
perforce (by necessity; because there is no other choice): done because circumstances leave no alternative. Source line (Titania, Act 2, Scene 1): “But she perforce withholds the lovèd boy.”
🌱 WORD ROOTS
distemperature breaks into the Latin prefix dis- (not, apart) and temperare (to mix in proper proportion, the root behind “temperature” and “temper”). Something distempered has lost its proper balance, whether that is a season, a body, or a mood.
perforce comes directly from Old French par force, literally “by force.” A thing done perforce is done because force of circumstance leaves no other option.
🔍 BEFORE YOU’RE TOLD: CONTEXT CLUES
Before you look at the meaning above, what in the lines right after “these are the forgeries of jealousy” hints at what forgeries means? Titania goes on to say the couple never met peacefully “but with thy brawls thou hast disturb’d our sport,” as if defending herself against an accusation. What kind of word would fit a defense against a false accusation?
📝 STUDENT DIRECTIONS
1
Add all five words and their meanings to the Word Study table (Section 2) of your Reading Journal.
2
Pick three of the words. For each one, write an original sentence using the word correctly. Then rewrite that sentence a second way, keeping the same meaning but changing the wording. Here is a model with a different word:
Your sentence: “The tired hikers rested perforce when the trail ended without warning.”
Your rewrite: “The tired hikers had no choice but to rest once the trail suddenly ended.”
3
Write one final sentence of your own using any one of the five words in a way that connects to this week’s question: whose account of events can we trust?

All five words and meanings recorded in the Reading Journal Word Study section.

Word Study: Words from Act 3
Assignment · 10 pts
📖 THIS WEEK'S WORDS (with the line they come from)
translated (transformed into something else): “Bless thee, Bottom! bless thee! Thou art translated.”
knavery (a dishonest trick): “I see their knavery. This is to make an ass of me.”
enamour'd (filled with love or delight): “Mine ear is much enamour'd of thy note.”
perforce (necessarily, whether wanted or not): “thy fair virtue's force perforce doth move me.”
derision (mockery, ridicule): “Scorn and derision never come in tears.”
🌱 WORD ROOTS
translated comes from the Latin trans- (across) joined to latus (carried). To be translated is literally to be carried across, from one form into another.
knavery comes from knave, an old word for a dishonest or tricky person, plus -ery, meaning an action or practice. A knavery is a knave's kind of trick.
derision comes from the Latin de- (down) joined to ridere (to laugh). Derision is literally laughing down at someone.
perforce comes from Old French par force, meaning "by force." Something done perforce happens because it must, not because anyone chose it.
🔍 BEFORE YOU'RE TOLD: CONTEXT CLUES
Before you look at the meaning above, what in the surrounding words hints at what enamour'd means? Think it through in your head or jot a note in your Reading Journal; you do not need to write this down for submission.

Original: “I see their knavery.”
Your rewrite: “I know exactly what dishonest trick they are playing.”
3
Then write one new sentence of your own using any one of the five words correctly. It does not have to be about the play.

🔮 WHAT YOU ARE DOING
In Act 3, Puck leads Lysander and Demetrius through the dark wood, mimicking each man's voice so they chase each other in circles without ever meeting. In VR you will stage that confusion, then record one lover's account of the night from inside it. This is direct practice for the module project, where you judge whose account of the night in the wood can be trusted.
📋 WHAT YOU WILL NEED

🎯 THE IDEA
This module keeps asking the same question in different scenes: whose account of events can we trust? This week you build the basic tool for arguing that question: an evidence paragraph. Word Study: Words from Act 4
Assignment · 10 pts · about 18 minutes
📖 THIS WEEK’S WORDS (with the line each comes from)
amazedly (in a state of astonishment or confusion): “My lord, I shall reply amazedly” (Lysander, 4.1). He is only half awake and cannot yet think clearly.
overbear (to overrule someone by greater force or authority): “Egeus, I will overbear your will” (Theseus, 4.1). The Duke uses his authority to set aside Egeus’s demand.
discourse (to talk about something at length): “I am to discourse wonders” (Bottom, 4.2). Bottom means he has amazing things to tell, though he never quite tells them.
transported (carried away, whether literally moved or figuratively overcome): “Out of doubt he is transported” (Starveling, 4.2). The mechanicals guess Bottom has been magically carried off somewhere.
paragon (a model of excellence; someone or something regarded as close to perfect): Flute corrects Quince, who meant to praise Bottom’s voice but used the wrong word (4.2).
🌱 WORD ROOTS
discourse comes from Latin dis- (in different directions) plus currere (to run). It originally meant to “run about” in talk, an extended discussion.
transported comes from Latin trans- (across) plus portare (to carry). To transport something is to carry it across or away.
paragon comes down through Old Italian and ultimately Greek, from a word meaning “to sharpen” or a testing stone used to judge the quality of gold. A paragon is still a standard other things get measured against.
🔍 BEFORE YOU’RE TOLD: CONTEXT CLUES
Before you look at the meaning above, look again at Lysander’s line: “My lord, I shall reply amazedly, / Half sleep, half waking.” What in the second half of that line hints at what amazedly means?

Original line: “Egeus, I will overbear your will.”
Your rewrite: The Duke decides to set aside Egeus’s objection and rule against him.
3
Write one new sentence of your own using any one of the five words correctly.

☐
Three rewrites keep the original meaning and use clear, correct wording.
☐
Your own sentence uses the word correctly.

Act 5, Scene 1, from the opening exchange between Theseus and Hippolyta through the start of the mechanicals' play. You read this text embedded on this week's lesson pages.
📖 READ & NOTICE · FIVE WORDS FROM ACT 5

These five words all come from Act 5, Scene 1. Add all five to your Reading Journal before you begin the steps below.

antique
Meaning: very old; belonging to an earlier time.
“I never may believe these antique fables, nor these fairy toys.” (Theseus)
abridgment
Meaning: a shortened form of something; here, a short entertainment.
“Say, what abridgment have you for this evening?” (Theseus)
premeditated
Meaning: planned or thought out ahead of time.
“Great clerks have purposed to greet me with premeditated welcomes.” (Theseus)
audacious
Meaning: bold, confident, showing no fear of consequences.
“I read as much as from the rattling tongue of saucy and audacious eloquence.” (Theseus)
constancy
Meaning: steadiness; the quality of holding firm and not changing.
“And grows to something of great constancy.” (Hippolyta)
🌱 WORD ROOTS
antique comes from the Latin antiquus, meaning “old” or “former.” Theseus uses it to dismiss the lovers' story as belonging to old superstition, not present fact.

premeditated comes from Latin prae- (“before”) plus meditari (“to think over, consider”). Something premeditated has been thought through in advance, the opposite of spontaneous.

audacious comes from Latin audax, from audere, “to dare.” The same root gives English the word “audacity.”

constancy comes from Latin constare (con-, “together,” plus stare, “to stand”), meaning “to stand firm.” Hippolyta's word choice matters: she is saying the lovers' story stands firm under examination.
🔍 BEFORE YOU'RE TOLD: CONTEXT CLUES
Before you look at the meaning above, what in the sentence hints at what abridgment means? Theseus asks for it right after asking “what masques, what dances shall we have, to wear away this long age of three hours.” What kind of entertainment would fit that request?
📋 ASSIGNMENT OVERVIEW
You will record this week's five vocabulary words in your Reading Journal and then practice them in your own writing. The goal is to use each word accurately enough that it shows you understand it, not just that you can copy a definition.
📝 STUDENT DIRECTIONS
1
Add all five words, their meanings, and the line each comes from to the Word Study section of your Reading Journal.
2
Pick three of the five words. For each, write one original sentence using the word correctly in a situation that is not from the play.
MODEL SENTENCE
"The audacious skateboarder attempted the highest rail in the park without a single practice run."
Notice: the model does not quote the play. It invents a situation that shows what the word means.
3
Write a short paragraph of 3 to 5 sentences describing any moment where two people disagree about whether to believe something. Use at least two of the five words naturally within your paragraph.
✅ SUCCESS CRITERIA
☐
All five words, meanings, and source lines are recorded in my Reading Journal.
☐
I wrote one original sentence for three words, each in a situation not from the play.
☐
My paragraph is 3 to 5 sentences and uses at least two of the five words correctly.
📤 SUBMISSION INSTRUCTIONS

Type your three original sentences and your short paragraph in the submission box. Keep the word list in your Reading Journal.

💡 THE IDEA

This Quick Write is a project feeder: what you write here builds directly toward your final essay about whose account of the night in the wood deserves to be believed. This week you practiced stating an opposing view fairly, then answering it. Now you will do it for real.

A strong argument does not pretend the other side does not exist. It states the other side honestly and then explains why the writer's own claim still holds up better.

2

Word Study: Words from the End of Act 5
Assignment · 10 pts
📖 THIS WEEK’S WORDS (with the line they come from)
abridgment (a shortened version of something, here a short entertainment): “Say, what abridgment have you for this evening?”
beguile (to charm or trick the time into passing pleasantly): “How shall we beguile the lazy time, if not with some delight?”
discretion (good judgment, the ability to tell what is wise or fitting): “True, and a goose for his discretion.”
consecrate (made holy or set apart for a special purpose): “With this field-dew consecrate,”
amends (something done to make up for a wrong or a mistake): “We will make amends ere long;”
🌱 WORD ROOTS
abridgment comes from the Latin root brevis, meaning “short.” To abridge something is to make it shorter, so an abridgment is a shortened version.
discretion comes from the Latin verb discernere, meaning “to separate” or “to tell apart.” Someone with discretion can separate a wise choice from a foolish one.
consecrate comes from the Latin root sacer, meaning “sacred,” joined with the prefix con- (“together, fully”). To consecrate something is to make it fully sacred or set apart.
amends comes from the Latin emendare, “to correct a fault,” built on menda, meaning “a fault.” To make amends is to correct a fault you caused.
🔍 BEFORE YOU’RE TOLD: CONTEXT CLUES
Before you look at the meaning above, reread the sentence: “True, and a goose for his discretion.” Theseus says this right after Demetrius calls the actor playing the Lion clever (“a very fox for his valour”). What in that exchange hints at what discretion might mean? Think it through in your head or jot a note in your Reading Journal. You do not need to write this down for submission.

1
Add all five words and their meanings to the Word Study section of your Reading Journal.
2
Pick three of the words. For each one, take the line it comes from and rewrite it in your own words, keeping the meaning but changing the wording. Here is a model with a different word:
Original: “We will make amends ere long.”
Your rewrite: “We will make up for this mistake soon.”
3
Then write one new sentence of your own using any one of the five words correctly. It does not have to be about the play.

All five words and meanings recorded in the Reading Journal.
☐
Three rewrites keep the original meaning and use clear, correct wording.
☐
Your own sentence uses the word correctly.

🔮 WHAT YOU ARE DOING
In the last lesson, you studied Puck’s epilogue, the moment the play steps outside its own story and speaks straight to you. In VR you will build that boundary between “inside the story” and “outside the story,” and stand at the exact point where Puck crosses it.

# Reading Journal Check: A Midsummer Night's Dream (Tier 2 checkpoints)

Build in: Canvas Assignment (file/OneDrive submission of the student's Reading Journal Word doc, or a "mark as done" completion submission). No custom code; Canvas-native. Tier: 2 (community / light). Two occurrences per module: a mid-module check around Week 3-4 and an end-of-module check at the close of Week 6, before the project. Light skim, not deep feedback. Purpose: confirm the Reading Journal is being built steadily, so the project has something to stand on. The journal is NOT collected weekly; this is the only deeper review. Metadata: Q3 / Module 4B.

No em dashes. This is a light-touch review. Do not write per-prompt feedback; score on completion and drop a one-line note where useful.

---

## What the student does

Share or upload your Reading Journal Word doc from your OneDrive course folder (LastName_MND_ReadingJournal_Module4B). You are not rewriting anything. You are showing your steady work so far.

  • Mid-module check (around Week 3-4): your journal should be current through Week 3 or 4 (through the verse-and-prose lesson and Bottom's transformation).
  • End-of-module check (end of Week 6): your journal should be current through Week 6, with a project claim taking shape in Section 5.

---

## What the teacher reviews (Sections 2, 3, and 5 only)

Skim three sections. Do not read every line.

  • Section 2, Word Study: Are the weeks' words present, with student-worded meanings and a citation in MLA format (author plus act.scene)?
  • Section 3, Weekly Reading Notes and Responses: Are the weekly prompts answered in full sentences, using details from the reading? Are the weeks up to date?
  • Section 5, Toward the Project: Is a claim forming about whose account deserves belief, with at least one or two cited pieces of evidence (especially at the end-of-module check)?

Ignore Sections 1 and 4 for scoring; they are the student's private working space.

---

## Completion rubric (simple, light)

| Rating | What it looks like | |--------|--------------------| | Full credit | All required weeks present in Sections 2 and 3. Prompts answered in full sentences with text details, cited in MLA format (author plus act.scene). Section 5 shows a claim (end-of-module: claim plus evidence). | | Partial credit | Most weeks present but some prompts are blank, one-word, or missing text details; Section 5 thin or just started. | | Minimal credit | Large gaps; several weeks empty; little or no Section 5 work. |

Suggested points: small completion value (for example, 10 points each check). Drop at most one brief note per student where it helps (for example, "Catch up Week 3 before the project" or "Strong evidence in Section 5, keep going"). No paragraph feedback.

---

## Teacher time note

Across 500 students this is a fast skim: roughly 30 to 45 seconds per journal at each checkpoint. Two checkpoints in the module. This is the deeper-review layer that lets weekly reading accountability stay on the auto-graded Check-up.

A Midsummer Night’s Dream: Your Creative Piece and VR Scene
Creative piece (your choice) + VR scene + reflection · spread across the project window
🎨 WHAT YOU ARE MAKING
Your essay makes the case for your position in words. This half of the project lets you show the same idea in a different form. You will create one piece that explores who tells stories in the play and who has to judge them, then build a short VR scene that stages one such moment, then write a reflection connecting both.
🖌 PART A: YOUR CREATIVE PIECE (choose one)
Pick whichever format fits what you want to say about the play’s storytellers:
Option 1: Staging Design
Design the stage for one storytelling moment in the play. Show where the teller stands, where the listener or listeners stand, and one visual detail that hints at whether the story should be believed. Your design can be hand drawn (photograph a physical piece) or created digitally.
Option 2: Character Map of Who Believes What
Build a visual map connecting each major storyteller in the play to the people who hear their account, with a note on whether that account is believed, doubted, or never really tested. A viewer should be able to look at the map and see the pattern across the whole play.
Option 3: Illustrated Scene
Illustrate one moment where a character tells their story, capturing the gap between what the character claims happened and what the audience actually saw. The illustration should let a viewer sense that gap without a caption explaining it.
All three options are equal in difficulty and graded on the same rubric. Choose the one that fits what you want to express.
🔮 PART B: YOUR VR SCENE
You have already built VR scenes in this module. Now use your VR headset to build one final scene that stages a moment where a character tells a story others must judge. This is not a costume-accurate recreation of the play. It is a space you build around the act of telling and judging a story.
📝 IN YOUR VR SETTING, DO THIS
1
Put on your VR headset and open the virtual environment. Choose any setting you like with enough open ground to arrange objects and labels.
2
Choose one storytelling moment from the play (Egeus’s plea, Titania’s tale of the changeling boy, Helena’s account of her friendship with Hermia, Bottom’s attempt to describe his vision, or the lovers explaining the night to Theseus and Hippolyta). Build a space with a teller and a listener, using objects or shapes to represent each.

Record this narration as part of your video, or as a short stand-alone audio or video clip if you captured a screenshot or wrote a description instead. This spoken part is required and graded for everyone; it does not trade off against a silent screenshot.
📝 PART C: YOUR REFLECTION (200 to 250 words)
Write a reflection of 200 to 250 words in Word. Answer these questions: Which character’s account did you choose to stage, and what did you learn about it by making your creative piece and VR scene? How did working with the moment in a different form change or deepen how you think about whose stories deserve belief? What do you still find hard or uncertain about judging a character’s account in this play?

All three parts are submitted together.

FINAL PROJECT · PART 1 OF 2
A Midsummer Night’s Dream: Your Literary-Analysis Essay
Literary-analysis essay · about 500 to 700 words · about 70 minutes of writing time, spread out · built from Quick Writes 3 to 6
📖 WHAT YOU ARE WRITING ABOUT
Almost every major character in A Midsummer Night’s Dream tells a story about what happened during one strange night in the wood. Egeus tells Theseus a story about Lysander bewitching his daughter. Titania tells a story about the changeling boy’s mother. Helena tells a story about her childhood friendship with Hermia. Bottom tries and fails to tell the story of his own vision. Theseus and Hippolyta openly argue about whether the lovers’ account of the night can be trusted at all. You have been building your analysis through Quick Writes 3, 4, 5, and 6. Now you pull that work into one clear literary-analysis essay.
🎯 FOCUS QUESTION
By the end of the play, whose account of the night in the wood should we believe, and what does the play suggest about why people tell the stories they tell?
📋 ASSIGNMENT OVERVIEW
Write a literary-analysis essay that answers the focus question. Choose one character’s account of the night (or argue that no single account is fully trustworthy) and make a claim about it. Support your claim with evidence from the play, cited with the author’s last name plus act.scene format, explain how each piece of evidence proves your point, address one counterclaim, and close with a conclusion about what the play suggests about storytelling. End your essay with one Works Cited entry for the play. Build it from your Quick Write 3 to 6 work in Section 5 of your Reading Journal. This is one half of your project; the creative and VR half is a separate assignment.
📝 STUDENT DIRECTIONS
1
Choose your position and write your thesis. Decide whose account of the night in the wood you find most believable, or argue that no single account fully earns trust. Write one clear sentence that states your position and hints at what the play suggests about why people tell the stories they tell. Put it at the end of a short opening paragraph that sets up the question.
2
Give your evidence and explain it. Use two or three specific moments from the play that support your thesis. Cite each one with Shakespeare’s last name plus act.scene format (for example, Shakespeare, 1.1), unless you already named Shakespeare in your sentence, in which case give just the act and scene (1.1). After each one, write a sentence or two that shows how it proves your point. Do not just cite the moment; explain what it means for your claim. Pull these from Section 5 of your Reading Journal.
3
Address a counterclaim. Name one reason someone might trust a different character’s account instead, using your Quick Write 5 counterclaim. Explain briefly why your case still holds.
4
Write a conclusion. End with two or three sentences that restate your thesis in fresh words and say what the play seems to suggest about why people tell the stories they tell.
5
Be honest about your reasoning. If a detail only partly fits your claim, say so. If two moments in the play seem to pull in different directions, acknowledge that. Naming where your evidence is strong and where it is less certain makes your essay stronger, not weaker.
📜 MLA CITATION REMINDER
Cite the play by the author’s last name plus act and scene, separated by a period: (Shakespeare, 1.1) means Shakespeare, Act 1, Scene 1. If you already named Shakespeare in your sentence, just give the act and scene: (1.1). Use this format for every piece of evidence, whether you quote directly or describe a moment in your own words. End your essay with one Works Cited entry: Shakespeare, William. A Midsummer Night’s Dream. Lesson 4.03 walks through examples if you need a refresher.
✅ SUCCESS CRITERIA
☐
A clear thesis names whose account you find most believable, or explains why none is fully trustworthy.
☐
Two or three pieces of evidence, each cited in author plus act.scene format.
☐
Each piece of evidence is explained, not just cited, and one counterclaim is addressed.
☐
A Works Cited entry for the play appears at the end of the document.
☐
A conclusion ties the essay back to why people tell the stories they tell.
☐

Week 1, "The Most Dangerous Game": disarming, naive, dread, imprudent, quarry

  • naive (adj.): too trusting; not yet wise to how the world really works
  • dread (noun/verb): a heavy, sinking fear; to fear something deeply before it happens

Create one Heading 2 block for Week 1, as below.

### Heading 2: Week 1, "The Most Dangerous Game" (Connell, 1924)

Reading-response prompts (answer in full sentences):

1. At the opening of the story, Rainsford says that the world is made up of two classes: hunters and huntees. By the end of the story, which class does he belong to? Use one detail from the story to support your answer.

2. Zaroff's island home is described in careful detail before we learn what he does there. Name one detail from that description that, looking back, hints at something dangerous. Explain what it hints at.

3. Zaroff uses polite manners and elegant surroundings throughout the hunt. What does that contrast between his manners and his actions add to the feeling of dread in the story? Explain in one or two sentences.

4. The story ends in one short, sharp sentence after Rainsford wins. Why do you think Connell ended it that quickly? What does that choice do to the reader?

My reading notes (characters, surprising lines, craft moves I notice, questions I have): - _______

Heading 1: Section 4, Craft, Characters, Theme

  • Craft moves I noticed: (term, what it was, where in the story)
  • Characters and what makes them work: (character name, one thing the author tells you directly, one thing the author hides or only hints at)
  • Suspense ideas: (a moment where suspense builds, and what the author did to create it: held back information, used short sentences, planted a clue)

## SECTION 5: Toward the Project (planning your own suspense story)

Heading 1: Section 5, Toward the Project

Your module project is a suspense short story you write yourself. Use this section to plan it step by step. Build it using your Quick Write as the first draft of a scene.

  • The project challenge: Write a suspense short story that builds tension and lands on an ironic twist ending.

Part A: Story Idea

  • My setting (where and when the story takes place): _______
  • The danger or problem that creates suspense: _______

  • What does the reader think is going to happen? (the expectation you will build): _______
  • What actually happens instead? (the twist): _______
  • What kind of irony does my twist use?
  • [ ] Situational irony: the outcome is the opposite of what was expected
  • [ ] Dramatic irony: the reader knows something the character does not
  • One thing I will hold back from the reader to build suspense (information I will not reveal until the right moment): _______

Part C: Structure Sketch

  • Opening (grab the reader; hint at danger without giving it away): _______
  • Rising tension (two or three things that increase dread): _______
  • The twist (the moment the reader realizes what was really happening): _______
  • Ending (brief and sharp, or slow and unsettling): _______

Part D: Author's Note plan

  • The suspense technique I am most proud of (and what I did): _______
  • The irony in my story (what the reader expected vs. what happened): _______

Keep this document in your OneDrive course folder all module long. Your teacher reviews Sections 2, 3, and 5 at the Reading Journal Check at the end of the module. You are not turning it in every day; you are building it as you go.

Week 1
Word Study: Words from The Most Dangerous Game
Assignment · ~18 min · 10 pts
📖 THIS WEEK’S WORDS
These five words come from Richard Connell’s story. As you read, find each one in context. Then add all five to Section 2 (Word Study) of your Short Story Reading Journal.
tangible (real; able to be touched or felt)
“...of a tangible menace.”
From: The Most Dangerous Game (Connell, 1924)
imprudent (unwise; not thinking ahead)
“It would be imprudent to antagonize the sailors.”
From: The Most Dangerous Game (Connell, 1924)
disarming (so pleasant it makes you feel safe, or reduces suspicion)
“...a disarming smile.”
From: The Most Dangerous Game (Connell, 1924)
indolent (lazy; not wanting to do much)
“...They had become indolent.”
From: The Most Dangerous Game (Connell, 1924)
quarry (an animal, person, or thing being hunted)
“What are the attributes of an ideal quarry?”
From: The Most Dangerous Game (Connell, 1924)
🔑 WORD ROOTS
Many English words are built from Latin or Greek pieces. Knowing a few common ones can help you figure out a word you have never seen before.
tangible
Comes from the Latin root tang-, meaning “to touch.” Something tangible is real enough that you could reach out and touch it, not just an idea in your head.
imprudent
Built from the Latin prefix im-, meaning “not,” plus prudent, from the Latin prudens, meaning “wise” or “careful.” Someone imprudent is acting in a way that is not wise or careful.
disarming
Built from dis-, meaning “away” or “removal,” plus arm, from the Latin arma, meaning “weapons.” To disarm someone literally means to take away their weapons; a disarming smile takes away your guard instead.
🔍 BEFORE YOU’RE TOLD: CONTEXT CLUES
Before you look at the meaning above, what in the surrounding words hints at what quarry means? Think it through in your head or jot a quick note in your Reading Journal; you will not turn this in separately.
📝 WHAT TO DO
1
Add all five words and their meanings to Section 2 (Word Study) of your Short Story Reading Journal.
2
Pick three of the five words. For each one, rewrite the line it comes from in your own words. Keep the meaning, but change the wording. Here is an example using a different word:
Original: “He was an animal at bay.”
Rewrite: “He was cornered, like a hunted creature with nowhere left to run.”
3
Write one new sentence of your own using any one of the five words correctly. The sentence should fit the meaning of the word.
✅ SUCCESS CRITERIA
☐
All five words and their meanings are in your Reading Journal.
☐
Three rewrites keep the meaning and use clear, correct wording.
☐
Your own sentence uses the word correctly and fits the meaning.
📤 SUBMISSION
Type your three rewrites and your own sentence in the Canvas text box below. Keep the word list in your Reading Journal.

VR Activity 1
What We Know vs. What We Don’t: A Suspense Station
Solo VR activity · ~25 minutes · 10 pts ~25 min
🔮 WHAT YOU ARE DOING
In “The Most Dangerous Game,” the scariest moments happen in the gap between what the reader knows and what the character suspects. In this activity you will build that gap in VR: a scene where something hidden is about to be discovered. You will save this work. It feeds your suspense short story project.
🎯 WHAT YOU WILL NEED
Your VR headset
About 25 minutes
Your memory of MDG’s hunt scenes
Your Reading Journal notes
⚡ HOW TO ENTER
Put on your headset and open your virtual environment. Choose any setting you like: a dense forest, a dark corridor, an open field at night, or anywhere that feels like something could be hiding.
📝 WHAT TO DO, IN ORDER
1
Place one object in your virtual setting that represents something HIDDEN or UNKNOWN. It could be a closed box, a shadowed corner, a door slightly open, or anything that suggests something is here but you cannot see it yet.
2
Add a second object that represents the CHARACTER who does not know yet. Label it with the character’s name or role.
3
Use sticky notes or labels to write: on the hidden object, write what the READER knows (what is really there); on the character object, write what the CHARACTER thinks is happening.
4
Stand back and look at the scene. Notice how the gap between the two labels is the source of suspense. Take a screenshot or record a short video of the full scene with both labels visible.
5
Write a short label or sticky note answering: What would have to happen for the character to finally discover the truth?
📤 WHAT TO SUBMIT
Upload your screenshot or video to Canvas. Then type two or three sentences: How did building this scene help you understand how the knowledge gap works in a suspense story?
✅ SUCCESS CRITERIA
☐ The scene shows a clear hidden object and a character who does not know.
☐ Both labels are visible: what the reader knows and what the character thinks.
☐ Your written reflection (2 to 3 sentences) explains how the knowledge gap creates suspense.

VR Activity 2
Story Planning: Design Your Twist
Solo VR activity · ~25 minutes · 10 pts
🔮 WHAT YOU ARE DOING
You have spent this week studying how “The Most Dangerous Game” and “The Landlady” build suspense and land a twist. Now it is your turn. In this VR activity you will plan your own suspense short story in three dimensions. Decide who your character is, what they do not know, and what the twist will be. Save this work: it is the foundation of your final project.
📋 WHAT YOU WILL NEED
Your VR headset · about 25 minutes · your Reading Journal notes from this week.
📍 HOW TO ENTER
Put on your VR headset and choose any virtual setting that fits the mood you want for your story. You are choosing the setting, not being assigned one.
📝 WHAT TO DO, IN ORDER
1
Place three objects in your virtual setting to stand for the three elements of your story: one for your CHARACTER (who they are, what they want), one for the HIDDEN TRUTH (the thing your character does not know), and one for the TWIST (the moment the truth is revealed or the outcome flips).
2
Label each object with a sticky note or label tool. For your CHARACTER: who they are and what they think is happening. For the HIDDEN TRUTH: what is really true that the character does not know. For the TWIST: one sentence on how the ending will flip expectations.
3
Use a whiteboard or drawing tool to sketch a simple 3-part story arc: Setup (character, setting, tension) / Rising Tension (what builds the suspense) / Twist (the reveal or surprise).
4
Stand in your setting and read your three labels. Ask yourself: Does the gap between the CHARACTER label and the HIDDEN TRUTH label create suspense? Would a reader feel dread knowing the hidden truth while watching the character not know it?
5
Take a screenshot or record a short video showing all three labeled objects and your story arc sketch.
📤 WHAT TO SUBMIT
Upload your screenshot or video. Then type three to five sentences: describe your three story elements (character, hidden truth, twist). You do not need the full story yet: just the core idea.
✅ SUCCESS CRITERIA
☐
Three labeled objects are visible in your screenshot or video, each representing one story element.
☐
The story arc sketch (setup, rising tension, twist) is visible in your screenshot or video.
☐
Your written description (3-5 sentences) identifies your character, hidden truth, and twist clearly enough to start writing.
