Weekly Workshop · Quick Write 1
Write a Short Suspense Scene
Composition · ~20 min · 15 pts
💡 THE IDEA
This week you studied how suspense writers create tension by controlling what the reader knows and what the character knows. Now you will try it yourself in a short scene. This scene does not need to be a complete story. It is a suspense moment: a character who does not know something the reader does.
📝 STUDENT DIRECTIONS
1
Choose a simple situation: a character approaches a door, opens a package, walks into a room, or picks up a phone. The situation does not matter. What matters is what the character does not know.
2
Decide on the hidden truth: What is behind the door, inside the package, in the room, on the phone? Write it at the top of your document as a note to yourself. Do not put it in the story.
3
Write 150 to 200 words: a suspense scene in which the character moves toward the reveal. Use at least one of the techniques from this week: a short sentence for a jolt, a long sentence to draw out a moment, a comma to create a pause, or a detail that foreshadows what is coming.
4
Do NOT include the full reveal in your scene. End at the moment of maximum suspense, just before the character finds out. This is the technique Dahl uses in “The Landlady.”
🔮 MICROSOFT 365
Create your Quick Write in Microsoft Word and save it to your OneDrive course folder. Name the file: LastName_SS_QuickWrite1. You will use this scene as raw material for your final suspense short story.
✅ SUCCESS CRITERIA
☐
150 to 200 words.
☐
A character who does not know something the reader does (the knowledge gap is present).
☐
At least one technique from this week: short or long sentence contrast, comma pause, or a foreshadowing detail.
☐
The scene ends before the full reveal.
☐
Saved in Word on OneDrive with the correct file name (LastName_SS_QuickWrite1).

# Reading Journal Check: Short Story Unit (Canvas Assignment, Tier 2 checkpoint)

Build in: Canvas Assignment (file/OneDrive submission of the student's Reading Journal Word doc, or a "mark as done" completion submission). No custom code; Canvas-native. Tier: 2 (community / light). One occurrence per module: an end-of-module check at the close of Week 1, before the final project is submitted. Purpose: confirm the Reading Journal has been built during the week so the project has something to stand on. The journal is not collected during the week; this is the only deeper review.

No em dashes. This is a light-touch review. Do not write per-prompt feedback; score on completion and drop a one-line note where useful.

---

## What the student does

Share or upload your Reading Journal Word doc from your OneDrive course folder (LastName_SS_ReadingJournal_Module5). You are not rewriting anything. You are showing your work from the week.

  • End-of-module check: your journal should be current through Week 1, with Section 5 showing a story idea and an irony/twist plan.

---

## What the teacher reviews (Sections 2, 3, and 5 only)

Skim three sections. Do not read every line.

  • Section 2, Word Study: Are the five MDG words present, with student-worded meanings and a line from the story?
  • Section 3, Weekly Reading Notes and Responses: Are the four reading-response prompts answered in full sentences, using details from the story?
  • Section 5, Toward the Project: Is a story idea present in Part A? Is there a twist plan in Part B, naming the type of irony and what the reader will expect versus what happens?

Ignore Sections 1 and 4 for scoring; they are the student's private working space.

---

## Completion rubric (simple, light)

| Rating | What it looks like | |--------|--------------------| | Full credit | Section 2 has all five words with student-worded meanings and a text line. Section 3 has all four prompts answered in full sentences with story details. Section 5 has a story idea (Part A) and a written irony and twist plan (Part B), with the irony type checked. | | Partial credit | Most sections present but some prompts are one-word or missing details; Section 5 has an idea but no twist plan, or a plan with no irony type identified. | | Minimal credit | Large gaps; several prompts empty; Section 5 blank or barely started. |

Suggested points: small completion value (for example, 10 points). Drop at most one brief note per student where it helps (for example, "Add story details to prompt 2 before the project" or "Strong twist plan in Section 5, keep going"). No paragraph feedback.

---

## Teacher time note

Across 500 students this is a fast skim: roughly 30 to 45 seconds per journal. This module has one checkpoint because Module 5 runs one week. This is the deeper-review layer that lets daily reading accountability stay on the auto-graded Check-up.

Reading-response prompts (answer in full sentences):

Heading 2: Week 2, Chapters 3-6

Reading-response prompts (answer in full sentences):

Sir Percy appears to everyone as a foolish, lazy fop. Find one moment where his behavior seems designed to make people underestimate him. What does this show about how he uses his reputation? 3. My reading notes (jot what you notice as you read: characters, surprising lines, questions): - _______

Heading 2: Week 3, Chapters 7-10

Reading-response prompts (answer in full sentences):

1. Marguerite has a brother, Armand, whose life is in danger. How does this put her in an impossible position between loyalty to her brother and loyalty to her husband (or to the Pimpernel's cause)? 2. What do you learn about what Marguerite revealed in the past that put a family in danger? How does she feel about it now? 3. In these chapters, what is your growing sense of Sir Percy's real character beneath the fop disguise? What clues has Orczy planted?

My reading notes (jot what you notice as you read: characters, surprising lines, questions): - _______

Heading 2: Week 4, Chapters 11-16

Reading-response prompts (answer in full sentences):

1. The plot stakes rise sharply. Describe one complication that makes it harder for the Pimpernel to carry out his rescue mission. 2. How does Chauvelin use Marguerite to try to trap the Pimpernel? What does this reveal about Chauvelin as an antagonist? 3. At this point, what do you think the novel is saying about the cost of keeping a secret? Use a detail from the reading.

My reading notes (jot what you notice as you read: characters, surprising lines, questions): - _______

Heading 2: Week 5, Chapters 17-22

Reading-response prompts (answer in full sentences):

1. How does Marguerite's understanding of Sir Percy change in these chapters? What does she realize, and what is the cost of that realization? 2. Word Study: Words from Paris and Dover

📖 THIS WEEK'S WORDS (with the line they come from)
execration (intense hatred or a curse): “A howl of execration greeted this tale.” (Ch. 1)
elusive (hard to catch or pin down): “the mysterious and elusive Scarlet Pimpernel” (Ch. 1)
audacity (bold, daring confidence): “a man whose pluck and audacity were almost fabulous” (Ch. 1)
sententiously (in a way that sounds wise or moral but is a bit pompous): “‘No,’ replied Mr. Jellyband, sententiously” (Ch. 2)
superstitious (believing in powers beyond reason): “a superstitious shudder ran down his spine” (Ch. 1)
🌱 WORD ROOTS
execration comes from the Latin root sacr (sacred): the same root in “sacred” and “consecrate.” To execrate something was literally to curse it by casting it out of what is holy.
elusive comes from the Latin root lud (to play): the same root in “illusion” and “prelude.” Something elusive keeps slipping away, almost as if it is playing a game of escape.
sententiously comes from the Latin root sent (to feel or think): the same root in “sentiment” and “consent.” A sententious remark is delivered like a weighty, thoughtful opinion, even when it is a bit pompous.
🔍 BEFORE YOU’RE TOLD: CONTEXT CLUES
Before you look at the meaning above, what in the surrounding words hints at what superstitious means? Think about what kind of feeling runs down someone’s spine right before that word shows up.

2
Pick three of the words. For each one, take the line it comes from and rewrite that line in your own words, keeping the meaning but changing the wording. Here is a model with a different word:
Original: “the mysterious and elusive Scarlet Pimpernel”
Your rewrite: “the unknown and impossible-to-catch Scarlet Pimpernel”

Then write one new sentence of your own using any one of the five words correctly. Your sentence must connect to something in Chapters 1 or 2.

In this activity you will use VR to think through the question from two angles, building the kind of thinking that will feed your argumentative essay. 📖 THIS WEEK'S WORDS (with the line they come from)
peremptorily (in a commanding, demanding tone that allows no argument): “Suzanne, come with me at once, I wish it,” said the Comtesse, peremptorily. (Ch. 5)
sangfroid (calm composure under pressure; French, meaning ‘cold blood’): “The Comtesse...trying to hide her excitement beneath more becoming sangfroid.” (Ch. 5)
inane (lacking sense; silly and empty): “his strong, clearly-cut mouth” was accompanied by “that perpetual inane laugh.” (Ch. 6)
equanimity (mental calmness and composure, especially in difficult situations): “nothing to disturb your equanimity,” rejoined Marguerite. (Ch. 6)
imperturbable (unable to be upset or excited; serene): “Blakeney, good-humoured as ever, had joined in the laugh...imperturbable good-humour.” (Ch. 6)
🌱 WORD ROOTS
peremptorily comes from the Latin root em (to take): the same root in “exempt” and “redeem.” A peremptory order takes away any chance to argue back.
equanimity comes from two Latin roots, equ (equal) and anim (mind or spirit): the same roots in “equal” and “animate.” Equanimity is literally an even, level mind.
imperturbable comes from the Latin root turb (to disturb): the same root in “turbulent” and “disturb.” Someone imperturbable cannot be stirred up or shaken.

Points

Poetry Workshop
Write in a Form: Sonnet or Villanelle
M365 Word document · about 25 minutes · 10 pts
🔮 WHAT YOU ARE DOING
In Lesson 2.03 you studied how a sonnet and a villanelle are each built. Now you will build one yourself. Choose one of the two forms and your own topic, anything you want a poem to be about. The frames below show you exactly where every line and every rhyme or refrain goes. They are empty frames to build inside, not poems to copy: every line you write should be your own.
💡 OPTION A: SONNET SKELETON (14 LINES)
Lines 1–4 (rhyme A B A B)
Introduce your topic and one first observation about it.
Lines 5–8 (rhyme C D C D)
Add a second angle, a complication, or a detail that develops the topic further.
Lines 9–12 (rhyme E F E F)
Push the idea one step further, or introduce a shift: a doubt, a contrast, or a change in the situation.
Lines 13–14 (rhyme G G)
The turn. In two lines, resolve, answer, or reframe everything the first twelve lines set up.
💡 OPTION B: VILLANELLE SKELETON (19 LINES)

First, write your two refrains: refrain A1 and refrain A2. These are the two lines that will repeat throughout the poem, so choose lines about your topic that can carry weight each time they return.

Tercet 1 (lines 1–3): line 1 = refrain A1 (new line), line 2 = new line, line 3 = refrain A2 (new line)
Tercet 2 (lines 4–6): lines 4–5 new, line 6 repeats refrain A1
Tercet 3 (lines 7–9): lines 7–8 new, line 9 repeats refrain A2
Tercet 4 (lines 10–12): lines 10–11 new, line 12 repeats refrain A1
Tercet 5 (lines 13–15): lines 13–14 new, line 15 repeats refrain A2
Closing quatrain (lines 16–19): lines 16–17 new, line 18 repeats refrain A1, line 19 repeats refrain A2

Choose a topic where returning to the same two lines makes sense: something you keep thinking about, something unresolved, something that will not let you move on. That is what makes the form fit the subject, the way it fit Robinson’s empty house.

📝 DIRECTIONS (follow in order)
1
Choose your form and your topic.
Pick sonnet or villanelle. Pick any topic of your own: a place, a person, a memory, a hobby, a worry, anything you can say something specific about.
2
Create a new Word document in OneDrive.
Open Microsoft Word (or Word online at office.com). Save it to your OneDrive folder for this class and name it LastName_SP_PoetryWorkshop.
3
Write your poem using the skeleton for your chosen form.
Follow the line count and structure exactly: 14 lines for a sonnet, 19 lines for a villanelle. If you chose the villanelle, keep your two refrain lines identical every time they return.
4
Add a one-sentence note below your poem.
Name the form you chose and explain in one sentence why that form fit your topic.
✅ SUCCESS CRITERIA
☐
The poem has the correct line count for the chosen form (14 for sonnet, 19 for villanelle).
☐
A villanelle repeats its two refrain lines in the right places; a sonnet's final two lines make a clear turn.
☐
Every line is the student's own writing about the student's own topic, not a line from Sonnet 18 or The House on the Hill.
☐
The one-sentence note names the form and explains why it fits the topic.
📤 SUBMISSION

Upload your Word document or attach it from OneDrive.

A Claim About a Character

🔮 WHAT YOU ARE DOING
In Lesson 2.04 you drafted a claim about one character from Chapters 3 through 6. Now you will develop that claim into a short argument paragraph: the claim itself, one or two pieces of evidence from the text, and a sentence explaining what your evidence shows. This paragraph is not a summary. It is the seed of the argument you will build in your final project.
📝 DIRECTIONS (follow in order)
1
Create a new Word document in OneDrive.
Open Microsoft Word (or Word online at office.com). Create a new blank document. Save it to your OneDrive folder for this class and name it: LastName_SP_QuickWrite2 (replace LastName with your own last name).
2
Write a heading at the top of the page.
Type your name, the date, and the title: Quick Write 2: A Claim About a Character. Press Enter once and then begin your paragraph.
3
Write your argument paragraph.
The paragraph should be 150 to 200 words and include three parts:
  • Your claim. One sentence that names a character and says something specific and debatable about what their behavior means. (Bring this directly from your Reading Journal.)
  • Your evidence. One or two specific details from Chapters 3 through 6 that support your claim. You may quote the novel directly or paraphrase it and include the chapter number in parentheses.
  • Your reasoning. One or two sentences that explain the connection: why does this evidence support your claim? What does it show about the character?
4
Upload a screenshot of your saved Word document to Canvas.

💡 WHAT A FINISHED PARAGRAPH LOOKS LIKE
“Sir Percy Blakeney’s performance as a fool is itself a form of courage, requiring more self-control than any open act of bravery. In Chapter 6, every person in London society has concluded that Percy is ‘hopelessly stupid’ (Ch. 6), yet in the same chapter Sir Andrew briefly catches Percy’s expression change to reveal ‘intense longing, deep and hopeless passion’ before it disappears again. This matters because maintaining the fool’s mask in the middle of a room full of people who know you requires constant effort. Percy is not absent-minded; he is exercising a kind of discipline that no one can see, and that is exactly the point.”
This model uses a different character than you may be writing about. Write your own paragraph. Do not copy or closely paraphrase this example.

📖 THIS WEEK'S WORDS (with the line they come from)
wistful (longing and a little sad): “she said, looking wistfully out to sea” (Ch. 7)
apprehensive (anxious, expecting something bad): “he threw a quick, apprehensive glance around him” (Ch. 7)
prepossessing (attractive, making a good impression): “the not very prepossessing little figure before her” (Ch. 8)
impassioned (expressed with strong feeling): “Marguerite had listened to Chauvelin’s impassioned speech” (Ch. 8)
imperceptible (too small or slight to be noticed): “the soft, almost imperceptible rustle of something on the floor” (Ch. 9)
🌱 WORD ROOTS
apprehensive comes from the Latin root prehend (to grasp or seize): the same root in “comprehend” and “prehensile.” To be apprehensive is to feel your mind grasping at something bad before it happens.
impassioned comes from the Latin root pass (to suffer or feel deeply): the same root in “passion” and “compassion.” An impassioned speech is full of strong feeling.
imperceptible comes from the Latin root cept (to take or seize): the same root in “accept” and “capture.” Something imperceptible cannot be taken in or seized by the senses.
🔍 BEFORE YOU’RE TOLD: CONTEXT CLUES
Before you look at the meaning above, what in the surrounding words hints at what wistful means? Picture where she is looking and how she is looking there.
📝 STUDENT DIRECTIONS
1
Add all five words and their meanings to the vocabulary table in Section 2 of your Reading Journal.
2
Pick three of the words. For each one, take the line it comes from and rewrite that line in your own words, keeping the meaning but changing the wording. Here is a model with a different word from the chapter:
Original: “she said, looking wistfully out to sea”
Your rewrite: “she murmured, her eyes full of longing as she gazed toward the distant water”
3
Then write one new sentence of your own using any one of the five words correctly.

🎯 THE IDEA
This week you watched three characters face versions of the same question: what do you risk, and for whom, and why? Now it is your turn to take a position. A thesis is not a summary. It is a claim you can defend with evidence from the text, a position someone might reasonably disagree with. Word Study: Words from Chapters 11–16
Assignment · 10 pts
📚 THIS WEEK'S WORDS (with the line they come from)

enigmatical (mysterious, impossible to explain): “...that enigmatical wayside flower.”

talisman (an object believed to bring protection or luck): “...that talisman which perhaps would save her brother Armand's life.”

impassive (showing no emotion; not reacting): He stood cold as a statue, impassive and still, his face showing nothing.

nonchalance (a relaxed manner that does not show worry): “...with the pretty nonchalance peculiar to herself...”

countenance (a person’s face or facial expression): Chauvelin and Percy study each other’s countenances throughout Ch 11–16, each searching for a sign the other cannot afford to show.

🌱 WORD ROOTS

enigmatical comes from the Greek root ainigma (riddle): the same root in “enigma.” An enigmatical flower is one that poses a riddle no one can solve.

impassive comes from the Latin root pass (to feel or suffer): the same root in “passion” and “patient.” With im- (not) attached, impassive means showing no feeling at all.

countenance comes from the Latin root ten (to hold): the same root in “contain” and “maintain.” A person’s countenance is literally what holds their expression together.

🔍 BEFORE YOU’RE TOLD: CONTEXT CLUES
Before you look at the meaning above, what in the surrounding words hints at what talisman means? Notice what it is supposed to do for Armand.

Original: “...that talisman which perhaps would save her brother Armand's life.”
Your rewrite: “...that small object she clung to, hoping it might somehow protect the brother she loved.”

Then write one new sentence of your own using any one of the five words correctly.

📖 THIS WEEK’S WORDS (with the line they come from)
presentiment (a feeling that something is about to happen): “a presentiment she could not very well have explained” (Ch. 17)
indefatigable (tireless, never giving up): “Her coachman, too, had been indefatigable” (Ch. 22)
dispassionately (without showing emotion, calmly): “She had spoken quietly, dispassionately, and with firm, unbending resolution” (Ch. 20)
poignancy (a deep, piercing feeling of sadness or emotion): “the child felt the poignancy of her friend’s grief” (Ch. 19)
sedulously (carefully and persistently): “sleep sedulously avoided her eyes” (Ch. 21)
🌱 WORD ROOTS
presentiment comes from the Latin root sent (to feel), with the prefix pre- (before): the same root in “sentiment” and “sensation.” A presentiment is a feeling that arrives before the thing it warns about.
indefatigable comes from the Latin root fatig (to tire): the same root in “fatigue.” With in- (not) attached, indefatigable means impossible to wear out.
poignancy comes from the Latin root pung (to prick or sting): the same root in “pungent” and “puncture.” A poignant feeling stings, the way a sharp point would.
🔍 BEFORE YOU’RE TOLD: CONTEXT CLUES
Before you look at the meaning above, what in the surrounding words hints at what dispassionately means? Notice what quality her firm, unbending resolution is paired with.

how near or close a danger is

Weekly Workshop / Quick Write 6
Quick Write 6: A Letter from Inside the Story
Composition · 15 pts
💡 THE IDEA
The whole plot of The Scarlet Pimpernel turns on one piece of writing: a letter. In Chapter 9, Chauvelin's spies seize a letter written by Marguerite's brother, Armand, and find it proves he is working against France. In Chapter 10, Chauvelin uses that letter as a threat: help him find the Scarlet Pimpernel, or the letter goes to the Committee of Public Safety and Armand is executed. A real letter, in this novel, decides whether a person lives or dies. Today you will write one yourself: a letter written by a character in this story, stating an opinion, registering a complaint, or requesting information, exactly the kind of real correspondence Armand's letter is.
💡 CHOOSE ONE LETTER TO WRITE
Option A: a business letter (registers a complaint or requests information)
Write as Marguerite. Address a formal letter to an official of the Committee of Public Safety. Either register a complaint about how Armand's private letter was seized and used against him, or formally request that the evidence against him be reviewed before any action is taken. Use a serious, businesslike tone throughout.
Option B: a friendly letter (states an opinion)
Write as Marguerite, imagining she could get word to her brother. Address a personal letter to Armand stating her honest opinion of what has happened since his letter was seized, and what she believes loyalty now requires of each of them. Use a warm, personal tone throughout.
📝 THE FOUR PARTS OF YOUR LETTER

Every real letter, business or friendly, has these four parts. Use this frame; do not skip a part.

1. Date and heading
Business letter: your name/title and the date. Friendly letter: just the date.
2. Greeting
Business letter: formal, for example "Dear Citizen [name]," or "To the Committee of Public Safety." Friendly letter: personal, for example "Dear Armand,"
3. Body (2 to 3 short paragraphs)
State your complaint, your request, or your opinion clearly in the first paragraph. Support it with a specific detail from Chapters 9 and 10 in the second. Close your point in the third.
4. Closing and signature
Business letter: formal, for example "Respectfully," or "Yours in earnest," then the name. Friendly letter: warm, for example "Your loving sister," then the name.
📝 STUDENT DIRECTIONS
1
Choose Option A (business letter) or Option B (friendly letter) above.
2
Write your letter using the four-part frame. Include the date and heading, the greeting, a body of two to three short paragraphs, and the closing and signature.
3
Ground the body in the novel. Reference at least one specific detail from Chapters 9 and 10, how the letter was seized, what Chauvelin threatened, or what Marguerite agreed to.
4
Your letter should be 150 to 200 words total, not counting the heading, greeting, and signature.
💡 M365 SKILL: FORMATTING A LETTER IN WORD
Create a new Word document and save it to your OneDrive class folder as LastName_SP_QuickWrite6. Use a blank line between your heading, your greeting, each paragraph of the body, and your closing, the way a real letter is spaced on the page.
M365 Skill You're Practicing: Formatting a business or friendly letter in Word (spacing, heading, closing)
✅ SUCCESS CRITERIA
☐
The letter clearly states an opinion, registers a complaint, or requests information, matching the chosen option.
☐
All four parts of the letter are present: date and heading, greeting, body, closing and signature.
☐
The tone matches the form chosen: businesslike and formal for Option A, warm and personal for Option B.
☐
The body references at least one specific detail from Chapters 9 and 10.
☐
150 to 200 words total, saved as LastName_SP_QuickWrite6 in your OneDrive SP folder.
📤 SUBMISSION
Canvas Assignment Name: Quick Write 6
Upload your Word document or attach it from OneDrive.

Week 7
Word Study: Words from the Ending
Assignment · about 18 minutes · 10 pts
📖 THIS WEEK'S WORDS (with the line they come from)
implacable (unable to be calmed or satisfied; relentless): “...bearing an implacable enemy to his triumph.” (Ch. 27)
peremptory (commanding; brooking no argument): “...he was saying in a low and peremptory whisper.” (Ch. 28)
ubiquitous (seeming to appear everywhere at once): “...that ubiquitous and daring Englishman could not hope to escape.” (Ch. 27)
indomitable (impossible to defeat or discourage): “Indomitable will to reach her husband...killed all sense of bodily pain.” (Ch. 28)
supposition (an assumption made without full proof): “As if to confirm this last supposition, the dull boom of a gun was heard.” (Ch. 30)
🌱 WORD ROOTS
implacable comes from the Latin root plac (to calm or please): the same root in “placate” and “placid.” With im- (not) attached, implacable means impossible to calm or satisfy.
indomitable comes from the Latin root dom (to tame): the same root in “domesticate.” With in- (not) attached, indomitable means impossible to tame or defeat.
supposition comes from the Latin root pos (to place): the same root in “position” and “compose.” With sub- (under) attached, a supposition is an idea placed underneath an argument, without full proof yet.
🔍 BEFORE YOU’RE TOLD: CONTEXT CLUES
Before you look at the meaning above, what in the surrounding words hints at what ubiquitous means? Notice what the characters keep failing to do about this Englishman.
📝 STUDENT DIRECTIONS
1
Add all five words and their meanings to the vocabulary section of your Reading Journal.
2
Pick three of the words. For each one, take the line it comes from and rewrite that line in your own words, keeping the meaning but changing the wording. Here is a model with a different word:
Original: “Indomitable will to reach her husband killed all sense of bodily pain within her.”
Your rewrite: “Her fierce, unbreakable determination to find Percy pushed away every feeling of physical pain.”
3
Then write one new sentence of your own using any one of the five words correctly, in a context outside the novel.
✅ SUCCESS CRITERIA
☐
All five words and meanings recorded in the Reading Journal.
☐
Three rewrites keep the original meaning and use clear, correct wording.
☐
Your own sentence uses the word correctly in a new context.
📤 SUBMISSION INSTRUCTIONS
Canvas Assignment Name: Week 7 Word Study
Type your three rewrites and your own sentence in the submission box. Keep the word list in your Reading Journal.

VR Activity 1
Suspense and Climax Station: Staging the Trap
Solo VR activity · about 25 minutes · 10 pts
🔮 WHAT YOU ARE DOING
In Chapters 27–29, three groups converge on the same coastal hut. Orczy uses physical space, darkness, and information gaps to build the tension. In this VR session you will stage that converging chase as a scene with labeled positions, then add analysis labels that name the craft moves Orczy is using. The scene will feed your project evidence.
📋 WHAT YOU WILL NEED
Your VR headset · about 25 minutes · your memory of Chapters 27–29 (reread the key scenes if you want the details fresh).
📍 HOW TO ENTER
Put on your VR headset and open the virtual environment. Choose any outdoor nighttime or open landscape setting you like. You need enough space to place three distinct groups of objects and a central landmark (the hut).
📝 WHAT TO DO, IN ORDER
1
Place a central landmark to represent the Père Blanchard’s hut (a small box or structure works fine). Label it: “The hut: Armand and the fugitives wait here.”
2
Place three groups of objects approaching the hut from different directions: one for Chauvelin and his soldiers (approaching from behind), one for Marguerite (following on foot in the dark), and one for Percy/the disguised cart (already at or near the hut, unseen).
3
Add three analysis labels, one for each group. Each label names one craft move from today’s lesson: dramatic irony, ticking clock, or sensory darkness. Write a brief note on the label explaining what Orczy is doing with that group (for example: “Dramatic irony: the reader knows Percy is the cart driver; Chauvelin does not.”)
4
Stand in the center near the hut and look at the three groups approaching. Note what it feels like to see all the threads closing in at once. Save this feeling for your project conclusion paragraph.
📤 WHAT TO SUBMIT
Take a screenshot or short video of your labeled scene (all three groups + the hut visible). Then type two or three sentences in the text box: which of the three craft moves do you think creates the most tension in Chapters 27–29, and why? Use the scene you just built to support your answer.
✅ SUCCESS CRITERIA
☐
The scene shows three distinct groups converging on the hut.
☐
Three analysis labels name real craft moves from the novel.
☐
A screenshot or video is uploaded with the short written reflection.

VR Activity 2
Static vs Dynamic Character Station: Building the Before and After
Solo VR activity · about 25 minutes · 10 pts
🔮 WHAT YOU ARE DOING
One of the most important things a reader can show in a literary argument is evidence of change over time. In this VR session you will build a "before and after" station for Marguerite Blakeney: objects and labels representing who she was at the start of the novel, and who she is by Chapter 31. The contrast becomes evidence you can reference in your essay conclusion.
📋 WHAT YOU WILL NEED
Your VR headset · about 25 minutes · your notes from Lessons 7.01 and 7.02.
📍 HOW TO ENTER
Put on your VR headset and open the virtual environment. Choose any setting you like. You need enough space to build two side-by-side areas: one for “Marguerite at the beginning” and one for “Marguerite at the end.”
📝 WHAT TO DO, IN ORDER
1
Build the “Beginning” side. Place objects or shapes that represent who Marguerite was in Chapters 1–6: celebrated, witty, seemingly in control of her world. Add at least one label with a word or phrase that describes her then (for example: “admired by London society”).
2
Build the “Ending” side. Place objects or shapes that represent who Marguerite is in Chapter 31: barefoot, exhausted, having risked everything. Add at least one label with a word or phrase that describes her then (for example: “willing to sacrifice her brother to warn Percy”).
3
Add a center label. Between the two sides, write a label that names the turning point: what single event or realization caused Marguerite’s change?
4
Stand between the two sides and look from one to the other. Think about what you would say if someone asked you: "Is the Marguerite at the end of the novel heroic?" Hold that thought for Quick Write 7.
📤 WHAT TO SUBMIT
Take a screenshot or short video showing both sides and the center label. Then type two to three sentences in the text box: In your own words, what changed Marguerite, and does that change affect your argument about what kind of courage the novel celebrates? These sentences can go directly into your Quick Write 7 conclusion paragraph.
✅ SUCCESS CRITERIA
☐
The station shows a clear before-and-after contrast for Marguerite, grounded in the novel.
☐
The center label names a specific turning-point event from the text.
☐
The written reflection connects the character change to the module’s argument about courage.

Quick Write 7
Conclusion Paragraph: What Does the Novel Argue?
Microsoft Word document · about 20 minutes · 15 pts
🔮 WHAT THIS IS
You have now read the whole novel and written six Quick Writes building toward an argument. This is the last piece before the Final Project: a conclusion paragraph that brings your argument to a close. In Week 8, you will organize all seven Quick Writes into an essay outline. In the Final Project weeks, you will revise and polish the full essay.
📝 DIRECTIONS
YOUR ARGUMENT QUESTION
Does the Scarlet Pimpernel’s disguise make him heroic, deceptive, or both? What kind of courage does the novel celebrate?
1
Open the Microsoft Word document where you have been writing your Quick Writes for Module 6. Scroll to after Quick Write 6.
2
Label the new section: Quick Write 7: Conclusion Paragraph
3
Write one conclusion paragraph (8 to 12 sentences). Your paragraph must include all four of these moves:
MOVE 1: RESTATE YOUR CLAIM
Restate your argument in fresh language. Do not copy your introduction. Use different words to say what kind of courage the novel values.
MOVE 2: YOUR STRONGEST EVIDENCE
Name one specific moment from Chapters 27 to 31 that best supports your claim. It does not have to be new evidence: it should be the moment you find most convincing.
MOVE 3: ACKNOWLEDGE THE COMPLICATION
The novel does not celebrate only one kind of courage. Name the complication your argument has to account for. Percy’s secrecy cost Marguerite something; Marguerite’s screaming nearly ruined the plan. A strong conclusion does not ignore this.
MOVE 4: CLOSING SENTENCE
End with one sentence that states why this argument matters beyond the novel. What does Orczy’s picture of heroism ask the reader to believe about real courage?
4
Save your file. Make sure all seven Quick Writes are in the same document: they become your source material for the Week 8 outline workshop.
✅ SUCCESS CRITERIA
☐
The paragraph includes all four moves: restated claim, strongest evidence, the complication, and a closing sentence.
☐
The evidence is specific: it names an event from the novel, not a general summary.
☐
The complication is acknowledged honestly, not minimized.
☐
All seven Quick Writes are in the same Word document, ready for the outline workshop.
📤 HOW TO SUBMIT
Save your document as: LastName_SP_QuickWrite7 (for example: Rivera_SP_QuickWrite7). Save it to your OneDrive and then upload the file to this assignment in Canvas.
⏩️ WHAT COMES NEXT
Week 8 is the outline workshop: you will arrange all seven Quick Writes into a full essay outline. After that, the Scarlet Pimpernel Final Project opens. At that point you will choose between the essay track and the Creative + VR track.

You have spent this week building the five parts of your argumentative essay outline. Today you do a final check, assemble all five parts into one clean Word document, and submit it. Conclusion: two or three sentences that restate your position in fresh words and say what the argument means beyond the plot. Does not repeat the thesis word for word.
☐
Format: each section is labeled, cover line is at the top, file is named correctly, saved to OneDrive, and submitted via Canvas.
📝 RUBRIC (20 points)
Criterion Full (5 pts) Partial (3 pts) Minimal (1 pt)
Thesis Takes a clear position, names the kind of courage, and gives a reason grounded in the novel. Position is present but reason is vague, or the kind of courage is not named specifically. A general opinion only; no specific reason or kind of courage named.
Evidence and Explanation Two or three specific moments from the novel, each with an explanation that says what it shows about courage and disguise. Evidence is present but explanation is only a restatement of the plot, or only one point is developed. Evidence is vague or missing; no explanation connects it to the thesis.
Counterargument All three moves present: other side stated fairly, something granted, and a clear response explaining why the argument still holds. One or two moves present; response present but does not fully address the objection. Counterargument is missing or only restates the thesis as a response.
Conclusion Restates position in fresh words and says what the argument means beyond the plot. Feels like an arrival, not a summary. Restates the position but only summarizes the evidence, or copies the thesis too closely. Conclusion is missing or is a single repeated sentence from earlier.

# Reading Journal Check: The Scarlet Pimpernel (Tier 2 checkpoints)

Build in: Canvas Assignment (file/OneDrive submission of the student's Reading Journal Word doc, or a "mark as done" completion submission). No custom code; Canvas-native. Tier: 2 (community / light). Two occurrences per module: a mid-module check around Week 4 and an end-of-module check at the close of Week 7, before the project. Light skim, not deep feedback. Metadata: Q4 / Module 6. Purpose: confirm the Reading Journal is being built steadily, so the project has something to stand on. The journal is NOT collected weekly; this is the only deeper review.

No em dashes. This is a light-touch review. Do not write per-prompt feedback; score on completion and drop a one-line note where useful.

---

## What the student does

Share or upload your Reading Journal Word doc from your OneDrive course folder (LastName_SP_ReadingJournal_Module6). You are not rewriting anything. You are showing your steady work so far.

  • Mid-module check (around Week 4): your journal should be current through Week 4 (rising stakes, Chauvelin's trap, the plot complications of Chapters 11-16).
  • End-of-module check (end of Week 7): your journal should be current through Week 7 (Chapters 27-31, the ending), with a project argument taking shape in Section 5: a thesis, at least two pieces of evidence with explanation, and a starting counterargument.

---

## What the teacher reviews (Sections 2, 3, and 5 only)

Skim three sections. Do not read every line.

  • Section 2, Word Study: Are the weeks' words present, with student-worded meanings and a line from the text?
  • Section 3, Weekly Reading Notes and Responses: Are the weekly prompts answered in full sentences, using details from the reading? Are the weeks up to date?
  • Section 5, Toward the Project: Is a thesis forming, with at least one or two pieces of evidence and explanation attached (especially at the end-of-module check)? Is a counterargument starting to appear?

Ignore Sections 1 and 4 for scoring; they are the student's private working space.

---

## Completion rubric (simple, light)

| Rating | What it looks like | |--------|--------------------| | Full credit | All required weeks present in Sections 2 and 3. Prompts answered in full sentences with text details. Section 5 shows a thesis (end-of-module: thesis plus evidence and a starting counterargument). | | Partial credit | Most weeks present but some prompts are blank, one-word, or missing text details; Section 5 thin or just started. | | Minimal credit | Large gaps; several weeks empty; little or no Section 5 work. |

Suggested points: small completion value (for example, 10 points each check). Drop at most one brief note per student where it helps (for example, "Catch up Week 2 before the project" or "Strong thesis in Section 5, keep adding evidence"). No paragraph feedback.

---

## Teacher time note

Across 500 students this is a fast skim: roughly 30 to 45 seconds per journal at each checkpoint. Two checkpoints in the module. This is the deeper-review layer that lets weekly reading accountability stay on the auto-graded Check-up.

FINAL PROJECT · PART 2 OF 2
The Scarlet Pimpernel: Your Creative and VR Piece
Creative work + VR scene + reflection · spread across the project window
🎨 WHAT YOU ARE MAKING
The Scarlet Pimpernel hides his true self behind a carefully built disguise, and so does the novel: the real story of who he is and what drives him only becomes clear slowly. In this part of the project, you will make something that shows what you understand about heroism and disguise in the novel, and then place that understanding inside a virtual scene.
🖌 PART A: YOUR CREATIVE WORK (choose one)
Choose one of the following. Each one asks you to show your understanding of the novel’s themes of identity, disguise, and courage:
●
A disguise and identity design. Design the Pimpernel’s disguise for one specific rescue scene in the novel, hand-drawn or digital. Label what the disguise hides, what it shows, and why that particular disguise fits that particular moment. The design must connect to the text.
●
A League of the Scarlet Pimpernel recruitment poster. Design a poster that could have been passed secretly among the League’s members. It must communicate the mission, the stakes, and what kind of person the Pimpernel is looking for, using only information from the novel. No character names that would expose anyone.
●
A scene illustration. Illustrate one scene from the novel (hand-drawn or digital) that you think best captures the theme of heroism in disguise. Write one or two sentences on the illustration explaining which scene it is and why you chose it.
●
A character map of the Pimpernel. Create a map or diagram showing how three or more characters in the novel see Sir Percy Blakeney, and how each one is wrong or limited. Use details from the book. The map should make clear how the gap between his true self and his public self drives the whole plot.
Whichever you choose, your creative work must be grounded in the novel. A viewer who knows the book should be able to see the connection immediately.
🔮 PART B: YOUR VR HEROISM SCENE
You have used VR several times this module to explore the novel’s themes: the world of the aristocrats at risk, the tense world of the chase, and the hidden courage of the League. Now build one scene that captures the idea of heroism in disguise.
📝 IN YOUR VIRTUAL SETTING, DO THIS
1
Put on your VR headset and open the virtual environment. Choose any setting you like: it can be a formal hall suggesting the English aristocracy, a dark road suggesting the escape route through France, a tense checkpoint scene, or any other setting from the novel’s world. The setting is your choice.
2
Build or arrange the scene so it shows the central tension of the novel: something on the surface that looks one way, and something beneath that tells a different story. You might use objects or labels to suggest two layers: what people see and what is actually true.
3
Add two labels or sticky notes to your scene. One should name what the scene looks like on the surface. The other should name what it actually reveals about heroism or disguise in the novel.
4
Record a short video or take a screenshot inside the virtual environment that captures both labels and the scene as a whole. If VR is not available to you, write a short paragraph describing the scene you would build in detail, including what the two labels would say.
5
Add a spoken explanation, 30 to 60 seconds long: narrate what your scene shows, in order, and name the one key point it makes about heroism and disguise. Record this narration as part of your video, or as a short stand-alone audio or video clip if you captured a screenshot or wrote a description instead. This spoken part is required and graded for everyone; it does not trade off against a silent screenshot.
📝 PART C: YOUR REFLECTION (200 to 250 words)
Write a reflection of 200 to 250 words in Word. Explain what you learned about heroism and disguise from building your creative work and your VR scene. What did making something help you see that reading alone did not? How do your creative work and your VR scene connect to your argument in the essay? Be specific: name the scene, the characters, and the ideas you were working with.
✅ SUCCESS CRITERIA
☐
The creative work is grounded in the novel and shows your understanding of heroism or disguise (not just a general picture of the story).
☐
The VR scene uses two labeled layers (surface and what it reveals) and is captured as a video, screenshot, or written description.
☐
The reflection is 200 to 250 words and connects the creative work and VR scene to the essay argument.
☐
All three parts are submitted together.
📁 M365 REMINDER
Write your reflection in Word, name it LastName_SP_ProjectReflection, and save it to your OneDrive course folder. Upload your creative work (a photo or digital file) and your VR video or screenshot with it.
📤 SUBMISSION INSTRUCTIONS
Canvas Assignment Name: Scarlet Pimpernel Final Project: Creative + VR
Upload three things: your creative work, your VR video or screenshot (or written description), and your Word reflection.
Due: end of Week 9.

Argumentative essay · about 500 to 700 words · about 70 minutes of writing time, spread out
📖 WHAT YOU ARE WRITING ABOUT
The Scarlet Pimpernel is a hero who operates entirely in disguise. His own wife does not know he is the man risking his life to rescue strangers from the guillotine. Readers have always debated whether that disguise is the heart of his courage or a sign of something more complicated. You have practiced this argument in Quick Writes 3 through 7 and built your outline in Week 8. Now you pull that work together into one clear argumentative essay.
🎯 FOCUS QUESTION
What kind of courage does the novel celebrate, and is the Pimpernel’s disguise heroic or deceptive?
📋 ASSIGNMENT OVERVIEW
Write an argumentative essay that answers the focus question. Take a clear position, state it as a thesis, support it with evidence from the novel and explain that evidence, raise the strongest argument against your view and answer it, then close with a conclusion. Build it from your Quick Writes 3 to 7 and the outline you completed in Week 8 (Section 5 of your Reading Journal). This is one half of your project; the creative and VR half is a separate assignment.
📝 STUDENT DIRECTIONS
1
Write your thesis. Decide your position on the focus question: is the Pimpernel's disguise heroic, deceptive, or something more complicated? Write one clear sentence that states your answer. This is your thesis. Put it at the end of a short opening paragraph that sets up the question for a reader who has not read the novel.
2
Give your evidence and explain it. Use two or three specific details or short quotations from the novel that support your thesis. Cite each one in MLA format: Orczy’s last name plus the chapter, for example (Orczy, Ch. 10). If you already name Orczy in your sentence, just give the chapter. After each one, write a sentence or two that shows how it proves your point. Do not just drop the detail; explain what it means. Pull these from Section 5 of your Reading Journal and from your Quick Writes.
3
Raise a counterargument and answer it. Name the strongest argument someone on the other side would make. For example, if you argue the disguise is heroic because it protects lives, a reader might point out that it also hurts Marguerite and hides the truth from the people he loves. State that fairly in a sentence or two, then explain why your position still holds.
4
Write a conclusion. End with two or three sentences that restate your thesis in fresh words and say what Orczy wants readers to understand about courage, disguise, and the cost of risking everything for strangers.
5
Add your Works Cited entry. At the end of your document, add one entry for the novel: Orczy, Baroness. The Scarlet Pimpernel. 1905.
6
Be honest about your reasoning. If a detail only partly fits your thesis, say so. Taking the other side seriously in your counterargument makes your argument stronger, not weaker.
✅ SUCCESS CRITERIA
☐
A clear thesis takes a position and answers the focus question.
☐
Two or three pieces of evidence from the novel, each cited in MLA format (author plus chapter).
☐
Each piece of evidence is explained, not just quoted or described.
☐
A counterargument is raised fairly and answered.
☐
A conclusion ties the argument back to the theme of heroism, courage, and disguise.
☐
A Works Cited entry for the novel appears at the end of the document.
☐
Writing uses clear paragraphs and is checked for clear sentences and spelling.
📁 M365 SKILL STEP
Before you submit, make sure you have:
☐ Written in Microsoft Word, opened from your school M365 account.
☐ Named your file LastName_SP_FinalEssay (example: Garcia_SP_FinalEssay).
☐ Set line spacing to double throughout the document.
☐ Added your name, the course, and the date in the upper left, then centered a real title above your writing (MLA-style heading).
☐ Used Heading styles for any section labels and a readable body font (Calibri 11 or Times New Roman 12).
☐ Saved it to your Optima > ELA > [your course folder] in OneDrive and confirmed it is there.
☐ Submitted through Canvas (your copy opens automatically, or use the OneDrive tab).
M365 Skill You’re Practicing: Using Track Changes and Version History (Word, OneDrive).
📤 SUBMISSION INSTRUCTIONS

Submit your Word document through Canvas. This essay and the creative plus VR half are graded together on one rubric.

quizzes.title: Module 4 Intro — Before We Begin
quizzes.description:
Welcome to Module 4. You will read The Outsiders by S. E. Hinton, a novel about two rival groups in 1960s Oklahoma and a teenager named Ponyboy who is trying to make sense of the world around him. The novel asks hard questions about loyalty, family, class, and what it means to hold on to something good. Before you begin, answer a few quick questions. There are no wrong answers here. Your first thoughts give your teacher a starting point.

Reading note: You will read from your own copy of the novel for this module. Each week's lessons will tell you which chapters to read. If you need help getting a copy, ask your teacher.

questions.text:
The Module Question, your first answer. Our question for this whole module is: **What divides the greasers and the Socs, and what does the novel say stays the same on both sides?

In two or three sentences, give your first answer. You have not read the book yet, so just say what you expect: what do you think divides groups of people, and is there anything that stays the same underneath those divisions? You will come back to this question many times.

(Survey, no scoring. Used to compare against the Q1 response on the module outro.)

Module objectives: check each box to show you have read it. By the end of this module you will be able to:

- [ ] Read all twelve chapters of The Outsiders in your own copy and follow the major events of the story. - [ ] Explain how Hinton uses a first-person narrator to shape the reader's view of the greaser-Soc divide. - [ ] Notice and name craft moves such as figurative language, foreshadowing, and point of view, and find them in the text. - [ ] Read and connect a poem (Frost's "Nothing Gold Can Stay") to a theme in the novel. - [ ] Write a literary-analysis essay: a claim about a theme, supported by evidence from your own copy, with explanation. - [ ] Build one Reading Journal all module long and use it to grow your project claim.

(Survey item. Acknowledgment, not a right answer; all boxes are correct to check.)
Group work opt-in. The final project can be done on your own or with one partner. Both paths get the same instructions and the same kind of feedback. Which do you want for this module?

answers.text: I will work on my own.
I would like to work with a partner (your teacher will help arrange this).
I am not sure yet; I will decide before the project opens.

questions.text:
One thing you are curious about. Name one thing about loyalty, class differences, friendship, or this novel that you are curious to find out. One sentence is fine.

(Survey, no scoring. Light engagement signal.)
"The team practices every Tuesday." What tense is the verb practices?

answers.text: future
past
present
past perfect

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Practices shows something that happens regularly now, so it is present tense.
questions.feedback_incorrect: If something is happening now or is always true, the verb is in the present tense. Look at when the action takes place.

questions.text: Which sentence uses the PAST tense correctly?

answers.text: She will return the book tomorrow.
He remembered every detail of the game.
They are leaving in the morning.
The door opens slowly.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Remembered shows an action that already happened, so it is past tense.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Look for the verb that shows something already completed or finished.

questions.text: "By the time we arrived, the movie had already started." The verb phrase had started is an example of:

answers.text: future tense
present tense
past perfect
future perfect

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Past perfect uses had plus a main verb. It shows one past event was already completed before another past event.
questions.feedback_incorrect: When had comes before a main verb, it creates the past perfect: something was already done when something else happened in the past.

questions.text: Which sentence correctly uses a SEMICOLON?

answers.text: She ran; because she was late.
He opened the door; a cold wind rushed in.
The list included; apples, oranges, and grapes.
She wanted; to go home.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Both parts are complete sentences, so a semicolon correctly joins them.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A semicolon joins two complete, independent sentences. Check that each side can stand on its own.

questions.text: Which sentence correctly uses a COLON?

answers.text: She needed: a good night of sleep.
The teacher explained: the rules carefully.
There are three rules: be honest, be kind, and be on time.
He ran: as fast as he could.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. The colon follows a complete statement and introduces the list that explains it.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A colon works after a complete sentence when a list or explanation follows immediately.

questions.text: "He had only one goal, one dream, one purpose: to finish the race." What does the colon do in this sentence?

answers.text: Joins two complete sentences.
Shows that a list of verbs is coming.
Introduces the explanation of what his goal was.
Replaces a question mark.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. The colon points to the answer for what the goal, dream, and purpose were.
questions.feedback_incorrect: What comes after the colon? It names the one thing the sentence has been building toward.

questions.text: A sentence uses had before a main verb: "She had finished her homework before dinner." What is had doing?

answers.text: It is the subject noun.
It is a helping verb that forms the past perfect.
It is a linking verb showing a state of being.
It is an adverb.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Had plus the main verb finished creates the past perfect. The helping verb shows the action was already completed before another past event.
questions.feedback_incorrect: When had comes before a main verb in the past tense, it is a helping verb forming the past perfect.

questions.text: Which mark belongs in the blank? "She had one request __ she wanted everyone to stay calm."

answers.text: a colon (:)
a semicolon (;)
a period followed by a capital letter
a comma

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Both parts are complete, independent sentences, and they are closely related, so a semicolon joins them well.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Both parts are complete sentences. A semicolon specifically joins two closely related independent clauses.

questions.text: A first-person narrator is one who:

answers.text: stands outside the story and observes all characters equally.
tells the story using "I" and shares only what they personally see and experience.
lets every character speak for themselves without any single narrator's perspective.
uses "we" to describe the experiences of a whole community.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. A first-person narrator uses "I" and tells the story from their own limited, personal point of view.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Think about the word "first person." This type of narrator uses "I"; they are a character in the story telling it from their own experience.

questions.text: Ponyboy, the narrator of The Outsiders, belongs to which social group in the opening chapters?

answers.text: The Socs
The teachers at his school
The Greasers
An unnamed neutral group

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Ponyboy identifies himself as a Greaser from the very beginning.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The narrator names his group clearly at the opening of the story. Which group does he say he belongs to?

questions.text: Which of the following BEST describes a simile?

answers.text: A direct comparison that says one thing IS another thing.
Giving an object or animal human qualities.
A comparison using "like" or "as."
Repeating a word at the start of several sentences in a row.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. A simile makes a comparison using "like" or "as." That word flag is what distinguishes it from a metaphor.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A simile is a comparison. What two signal words tell a reader it is a simile rather than a metaphor?

questions.text: Read this original example: "Her voice was as sharp as broken glass." This sentence uses:

answers.text: Personification
A metaphor
A simile
Hyperbole

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. "As sharp as broken glass" uses "as" to link two things in a comparison, making it a simile.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Look for the comparison signal word: "as." When a comparison uses "like" or "as," it is a simile.

questions.text: "She had finished the project before the deadline arrived." What tense is the verb phrase had finished?

answers.text: Present tense
Future perfect
Simple past
Past perfect

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Past perfect uses "had" plus a main verb. It shows one past action was already completed before another past action happened.
questions.feedback_incorrect: When "had" comes before a main verb, it creates a special past form. What tense shows that one past event was already done when another past event occurred?

questions.text: Which sentence correctly uses a COLON?

answers.text: She ran: because she was late.
He called: his best friend immediately.
The coach announced three rules: arrive early, work hard, and respect everyone.
They left: before the show ended.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. The colon follows a complete sentence and introduces the list that explains the three rules.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A colon introduces a list or explanation. It must follow a complete sentence. Which sentence has a complete statement before the colon AND a true list after it?

questions.text: A reader INFERS something about a narrator when:

answers.text: The narrator states a fact directly in plain language.
A character says the same thing twice for emphasis.
The reader pieces together meaning from details the narrator does not state directly.
The author includes a note explaining what a scene means.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Inference is what a reader builds from clues and details, not from direct statements.
questions.feedback_incorrect: When a reader infers, they are going beyond what is stated. They are reading between the lines, drawing a conclusion the narrator never says outright.

questions.text: Which sentence BEST demonstrates a past perfect verb?

answers.text: He will finish the report by Thursday.
They are leaving for the game right now.
She had already eaten by the time dinner was served.
The lights turned off at midnight.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. "Had already eaten" uses "had" plus the main verb to show that eating was completed before the other past event (dinner being served).
questions.feedback_incorrect: Past perfect uses "had" before a main verb to show one past event was completed before another. Which sentence shows that?

questions.text: "The old car rattled and sighed as it climbed the hill." The word "sighed" gives the car a human quality. This is an example of:

answers.text: A simile
A colon used for emphasis
Alliteration
Personification

questions.feedback_correct: Right. "Sighed" attributes a human emotion or action to an object. That is personification.
questions.feedback_incorrect: When a non-human thing is described as doing or feeling something only a person would do or feel, what literary device is being used?

questions.text: Which sentence correctly uses a SEMICOLON?

answers.text: She finished early; because she had prepared well.
The test was hard; she had studied for it every night, though.
He wanted three things; loyalty, honesty, and courage.
The door opened; a cold wind swept through the room.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Both parts are complete, closely related sentences. A semicolon correctly joins two independent clauses.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A semicolon joins two complete, independent sentences. Check each option: can both sides stand alone as complete sentences?

questions.text:
Parts of Speech

Which word is the subject noun in this sentence?

"The small brown bird sang a cheerful song."

answers.text: small
bird
sang
song

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Bird is the noun that performs the action. It answers "who or what sang?" so bird is the subject noun.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Find the verb sang, then ask "who or what sang?" The noun that answers that question is the subject noun.

questions.text:
Parts of Speech

In this sentence, which word is an adverb?

"She carefully placed the vase on the wooden shelf."

answers.text: carefully
wooden
vase
placed

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Carefully tells how she placed the vase. It answers "placed how?" so it is an adverb.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Find the verb placed and ask "placed how?" The word that answers that question is the adverb.

questions.text:
Parts of Speech

The words a, an, and the belong to which category?

answers.text: pronouns
prepositions
article adjectives
interjections

questions.feedback_correct: Right. A, an, and the are article adjectives. They point to a noun and answer "which one."
questions.feedback_incorrect: A, an, and the always point to a noun. That makes them article adjectives.

questions.text:
Parts of Speech

In this sentence, which word is a conjunction?

"Marcus and his brother walked slowly down the long road."

answers.text: slowly
down
long
and

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. And joins "Marcus" and "his brother." Connecting two parts of a sentence is a conjunction's job.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Look for the word that connects two parts of the sentence. That connecting word is a conjunction.

questions.text:
Parts of Speech

What question do you ask to find the subject in any sentence?

answers.text: What kind? Which one? How many?
How? When? Where? To what extent?
Who or what [verb]?
What is the action being received?

questions.feedback_correct: Right. To find the subject, find the verb first and then ask "who or what [verb]?" The noun or pronoun that answers is the subject.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The subject-finding question is "who or what [verb]?" using the verb you already found in the sentence.

questions.text:
Active and Passive Voice

Which sentence is in active voice?

answers.text: The trophy was awarded to the team by the judges.
The window had been broken before we arrived.
The judges awarded the trophy to the team.
The cake was eaten before the party ended.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. The judges (subject) are performing the action of awarding. When the subject acts, the sentence is in active voice.
questions.feedback_incorrect: In active voice the subject performs the action. Which sentence has the subject doing something rather than having something done to it?

questions.text:
Active and Passive Voice

In a passive-voice sentence, the verb usually includes:

answers.text: an action verb with no helping verb
a helping verb paired with a past-participle main verb
two action verbs in a row
an article adjective before the verb

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Passive voice combines a helping verb (was, were, is, are, has been, etc.) with a past-participle main verb.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Look for the combination of a helping verb plus a past-participle main verb. That pattern is the signal for passive voice.

questions.text:
Active and Passive Voice

Which sentence is in passive voice?

answers.text: The dog chased the squirrel up the tree.
My uncle builds furniture in his workshop.
The mayor signed the new agreement yesterday.
The new agreement was signed by the mayor.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. The agreement (subject) did not sign anything. It was acted upon. "Was signed" is a helping verb plus past-participle main verb, so this is passive voice.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Ask whether the subject is doing the action or receiving it. "Was signed by the mayor" puts the agreement as the receiver, not the doer.

questions.text:
Active and Passive Voice

You want to emphasize what happened rather than who did it. Which voice is usually the better choice?

answers.text: Passive voice
Active voice
Both work equally in all situations.
Neither. You should use a question instead.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Passive voice shifts attention to the action or the result. That is useful when the doer is unknown or less important than what happened.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Think about which voice hides the doer and puts the spotlight on what happened.

questions.text:
Active and Passive Voice

Change this passive sentence to active voice:

"The old book was found by a student."

Which version is the correct active-voice rewrite?

answers.text: The old book found a student.
A student was finding the old book.
The old book had been found.
A student found the old book.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Moving the doer (a student) to the subject position and using the simple past action verb (found) converts the sentence to active voice.
questions.feedback_incorrect: In active voice the doer becomes the subject and performs the action directly. Who found the book? Make that the subject.

questions.text: In Chapters 3 and 4, which of the following best describes the relationship between the greasers and the Socs?

answers.text: They have lived in peace for many years.
They compete in organized sports.
There is ongoing tension and rivalry between the two groups, often turning violent.
They ignore each other completely.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. The divide between the greasers and the Socs is the central social conflict of the novel, and Chapters 3 and 4 show that tension reaching a breaking point.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Reread the chapters thinking about how the two groups interact. What kind of relationship is this?

questions.text: At the end of Chapter 4, Ponyboy and Johnny make a decision. Which best describes what they choose to do?

answers.text: They turn themselves in to the police immediately.
They decide to run and seek help from a trusted older friend.
They go home and pretend nothing happened.
They ask Cherry Valance for help.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Ponyboy and Johnny choose to flee and turn to an older friend for advice rather than face the immediate consequences.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Reread the final pages of Chapter 4. What do Ponyboy and Johnny decide to do after the confrontation?

questions.text: In a story, a "signal" is best described as:

answers.text: A character's name that hints at the plot.
A chapter title that summarizes the events.
A conversation between two characters at the beginning.
A detail that foreshadows or hints at what is coming later in the story.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. A signal is a detail the author places early so that when a big event arrives, it feels like it was building all along.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Think about what you practiced this week: small details that hint at what is coming. What is the term for that kind of detail?

questions.text: Which of these best describes an analytical claim about a character?

answers.text: "Johnny is a greaser who lives in the same neighborhood as Ponyboy."
"In Chapter 4, something serious happens and the characters have to run."
"Ponyboy narrates the story in first person."
"Johnny's decision in Chapter 4 shows that his loyalty to Ponyboy is more powerful than his fear of consequences."

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. A claim takes a position about what a detail means. The other options describe facts or events without interpreting them.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A claim is not a summary or a fact. It says what you think a detail or event reveals. Which option does that?

questions.text: The tension in Chapter 3 contributes to the crisis in Chapter 4. What does this pattern suggest about how the novel is structured?

answers.text: Events in this novel happen randomly, without any connection to each other.
The novel builds its big events gradually, using earlier scenes to prepare the reader.
Earlier events are not connected to what happens later.
Chapter 4 would make sense without reading Chapter 3 first.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. The way Chapter 3 builds tension that erupts in Chapter 4 is an example of the novel's structure: earlier events prepare you for later ones.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Think about the relationship between the chapters. Does Chapter 4 come out of nowhere, or does Chapter 3 set it up?

questions.text: Which word is the adverb in "The small crowd gathered quietly near the old fountain"?

answers.text: quietly
small
gathered
near

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. "Quietly" tells how the crowd gathered. It answers "how" about the verb, so it is an adverb.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Find the verb "gathered" and ask "gathered how?" The word that answers that question is the adverb.

questions.text: Which sentence is in passive voice?

answers.text: The coach selected the starting lineup before the game.
My sister baked a birthday cake yesterday.
The decision was made by the committee.
A student left a backpack in the hallway.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. "Was made" is a helping verb plus a past-participle main verb, and the subject (decision) is receiving the action, not performing it. That is passive voice.
questions.feedback_incorrect: In passive voice the subject receives the action. Look for a helping verb before the main verb. Which sentence fits that pattern?

questions.text: The Outsiders is narrated in first person by Ponyboy. What does that mean for a reader who wants to understand all the characters fairly?

answers.text: We can trust everything Ponyboy says about every character completely.
The story is told by an outside narrator who knows everyone's thoughts.
Ponyboy's view is the only perspective in the novel, so we only see what he sees and understands.
The first-person narrator means the story happened exactly as written.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. A first-person narrator shows us events through one character's eyes. That means Ponyboy's understanding, feelings, and limitations shape everything we know.
questions.feedback_incorrect: First person means one character narrates with "I." What does that mean for how much we can know about other characters?

questions.text:
Read this sentence: "The frightened boy hid silently behind the old wooden door."

Which part of the sentence is a prepositional phrase?

answers.text: The frightened boy
hid silently
behind the old wooden door
frightened boy hid

questions.text:
Read this sentence: "The dog barked, and the boys stayed still."

What type of sentence is this?

answers.text: Simple
Compound
Complex
Fragment

questions.text:
Read this sentence: "Because the rain started, the two boys ran inside."

What type of sentence is this?

answers.text: Simple
Compound
Complex
Run-on

questions.text: In the sentence "The restless boy read quietly," what part of speech is the word "quietly"?

answers.text: Adjective, because it describes something in the sentence
Adverb, because it answers "How?" about the verb
Preposition, because it comes after the verb
Noun, because it names something

questions.text: A student wrote: "Because she was tired." Can this stand alone as a complete sentence?

answers.text: Yes, because it has a subject and a verb
No, because it is a dependent clause that needs an independent clause to complete it
Yes, if you add a period at the end
No, because it has no subject

questions.text: In Chapters 5–6, where do Ponyboy and Johnny hide out while they wait for help?

answers.text: A barn on the edge of town
An abandoned church on a hill
Dally's apartment
A friend's basement

questions.text: Robert Frost's poem "Nothing Gold Can Stay" describes something beautiful and golden that cannot last. In the context of Chapters 5–6, what does "gold" most likely represent for Ponyboy?

answers.text: Actual gold or money
The greasers' loyalty to each other
Innocence, beauty, and the part of youth that cannot be held on to
The sunrise itself, and nothing more

questions.text: Which of the following best describes how Johnny changes during Chapters 5–6?

answers.text: He becomes more frightened and unable to function.
He turns against Ponyboy and wants to give himself up immediately.
He becomes calmer and more decisive, taking charge of practical decisions.
He spends the whole time sleeping.

questions.text:
Read this sentence: "Although the boys were hungry, they waited quietly."

What type of sentence is this?

answers.text: Simple
Compound
Complex
Fragment

questions.text: In the sentence "He spoke softly to the nervous dog," what part of speech is the word "softly"?

answers.text: Adjective, because it describes the dog
Adverb, because it answers "How?" about the verb
Noun, because it follows the verb
Preposition, because it comes before a noun

questions.text:
Which word in this sentence needs to be capitalized?

"Every wednesday, the boys met at the park."

answers.text: every
boys
wednesday
park

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Wednesday is the name of a specific day of the week, so it is a proper noun and must be capitalized.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Look for the word that names a specific day, month, or proper noun. Days of the week are always capitalized.

questions.text: Which sentence correctly capitalizes the title used before a name?

answers.text: She spoke with officer Torres about the report.
She spoke with Officer Torres about the report.
She Spoke With officer Torres About The Report.
she spoke with officer torres about the report.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. A title used directly before a person's name is capitalized: Officer Torres.
questions.feedback_incorrect: When a title comes right before a specific person's name, it is capitalized. When it stands alone, it is lowercase.

questions.text: Which sentence uses the correct end mark?

answers.text: Did the hospital allow visitors every day.
Did the hospital allow visitors every day?
Did the hospital allow visitors every day!
Did the hospital allow visitors every day;

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. The sentence asks a question, so it ends with a question mark.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Check the purpose of the sentence. A sentence that asks something is interrogative and ends with a question mark.

questions.text:
Which word in this sentence should NOT be capitalized?

"Two boys from tulsa waited outside Memorial Hospital."

answers.text: Boys
tulsa (needs to be capitalized)
Boys
Memorial Hospital

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Boys is a common noun; it should not be capitalized in the middle of a sentence.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Tulsa and Memorial Hospital are proper nouns and must be capitalized. Boys is a common noun used in the middle of a sentence: no capital letter needed.

questions.text: Which sentence uses title punctuation correctly for a novel?

answers.text: He had read "The Outsiders" twice.
He had read THE OUTSIDERS twice.
He had read The Outsiders twice.
He had read The Outsiders twice.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. A novel is a long work and its title is italicized (or underlined in handwriting).
questions.feedback_incorrect: Long works like novels, films, and albums get italics (or underlining in handwriting). Quotation marks are for short works like poems and short stories.

questions.text: Which sentence uses title punctuation correctly for a poem?

answers.text: She memorized Nothing Gold Can Stay for class.
She memorized Nothing Gold Can Stay for class.
She memorized "Nothing Gold Can Stay" for class.
She memorized NOTHING GOLD CAN STAY for class.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. A poem is a short work, so its title goes in quotation marks.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Short works like poems, short stories, and song titles go in quotation marks. Italics are for long works like novels and films.

questions.text: Which sentence correctly introduces a quotation with a signal phrase?

answers.text: The narrator recalls "I kept walking and did not look back." (Ch. 7)
The narrator recalls, "I kept walking and did not look back." (Ch. 7)
The narrator recalls. "I kept walking and did not look back." (Ch. 7)
The narrator recalls "I kept walking and did not look back" (Ch. 7).

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. A comma follows the signal phrase before the opening quotation mark. The period goes inside the closing quotation mark, before the citation.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A signal phrase is followed by a comma, then the opening quotation mark. The period belongs inside the closing quotation mark.

questions.text: Where does the period go when a sentence ends with a quoted passage?

answers.text: After the closing quotation mark, outside it.
Before the opening quotation mark.
Inside the closing quotation mark.
There is no period; the quotation mark ends the sentence.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. In American English, the period goes inside the closing quotation mark.
questions.feedback_incorrect: In American English, periods and commas always go inside the closing quotation mark, not outside it.

questions.text: Which version correctly cites a quotation from Chapter 8?

answers.text: "He said nothing at all" (Ch. 8).
"He said nothing at all." (Ch. 8)
"He said nothing at all" (Ch. 8.)
He said nothing at all (Ch. 8).

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. The period follows the parenthetical citation: close the quotation mark, then the citation, then the period.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The correct order is: closing quotation mark, then the citation in parentheses, then the period. The period does not go inside the quote when there is a citation following it.

questions.text: A sentence that gives a strong command ends with:

answers.text: A comma
A question mark
A semicolon
A period or an exclamation mark

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Imperative sentences (commands or requests) typically end with a period; when the command is urgent or emotional, an exclamation mark is correct.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A command is an imperative sentence. It ends with a period for a calm instruction or an exclamation mark for a forceful or urgent one.

questions.text: In Chapters 7 and 8 of The Outsiders, the story slows down and focuses on characters in the hospital. What best describes the main emotional tone of these chapters?

answers.text: Excited and triumphant
Tense and hopeful at the same time
Funny and relaxed
Angry and loud

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. These chapters balance fear, hope, and quiet loyalty as characters wait and worry.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Think about the mood when characters are waiting at the hospital. It is not triumphant or relaxed.

questions.text: In The Outsiders, the theme of loyalty is mostly shown through:

answers.text: Characters winning fights
